text:
(F) Pope Saint Damasus I

“Likewise it is decreed . . . that it ought to be announced that . . . the holy Roman Church has been placed at the forefront not by the conciliar decisions of other churches, but has received the primacy by the evangelic voice of our Lord and Savior, who says: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it; and I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven . . . ’ [Matt. 16:18–19]. The first see, therefore, is that of Peter the apostle, that of the Roman Church, which has neither stain nor blemish nor anything like it” (Decree of Damasus 3 [A.D. 382]).

(G) Saint Jerome

“‘But,’ you [Jovinian] will say, ‘it was on Peter that the Church was founded’ [Matt. 16:18]. Well . . . one among the twelve is chosen to be their head in order to remove any occasion for division” (Against Jovinian 1:26 [A.D. 393]).

(H) Pope Saint Innocent I

 “In seeking the things of God . . . you have acknowledged that judgment is to be referred to us [the pope], and have shown that you know that is owed to the Apostolic See [Rome], if all of us placed in this position are to desire to follow the apostle himself [Peter] from whom the episcopate itself and the total authority of this name have emerged” (Letters 29:1 [A.D. 408]).

(I) Saint Augustine

“Among these [apostles] Peter alone almost everywhere deserved to represent the whole Church. Because of that representation of the Church, which only he bore, he deserved to hear ‘I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’” (Sermons 295:2 [A.D. 411]).

“Some things are said which seem to relate especially to the apostle Peter, and yet are not clear in their meaning unless referred to the Church, which he is acknowledged to have represented in a figure on account of the primacy which he bore among the disciples. Such is ‘I will give unto you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,’ and other similar passages” (Commentary on Psalm 108 1 [A.D. 415]).

“Who is ignorant that the first of the apostles is the most blessed Peter?” (Commentary on John 56:1 [A.D. 416]).

(J) Council of Ephesus 

“Philip, presbyter and legate of [Pope Celestine I] said: ‘We offer our thanks to the holy and venerable synod, that when the writings of our holy and blessed pope had been read to you . . . you joined yourselves to the holy head also by your holy acclamations. For your blessedness is not ignorant that the head of the whole faith, the head of the apostles, is blessed Peter the apostle’” (Acts of the Council, session 2 [A.D. 431]).
“Philip, the presbyter and legate of the Apostolic See [Rome] said: ‘There is no doubt, and in fact it has been known in all ages, that the holy and most blessed Peter, prince and head of the apostles, pillar of the faith, and foundation of the Catholic Church, received the keys of the kingdom from our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior and Redeemer of the human race, and that to him was given the power of loosing and binding sins: who down even to today and forever both lives and judges in his successors’” (ibid., session 3).

(K) Pope Saint Leo I

“Our Lord Jesus Christ . . . has placed the principal charge on the blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, and from him as from the head wishes his gifts to flow to all the body, so that anyone who dares to secede from Peter’s solid rock may understand that he has no part or lot in the divine mystery. He wished him who had been received into partnership in his undivided unity to be named what he himself was, when he said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ [Matt. 16:18], that the building of the eternal temple might rest on Peter’s solid rock, strengthening his Church so surely that neither could human rashness assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it” (Letters 10:1 [A.D. 445).

NEWS RELEASE: Suspect in Thornton officer shooting arrested

Luis Arebalo, the suspect in the Oct. 11 shooting of a Thornton Police officer, is in custody.

On Oct. 13 at about 5:30 p.m., Thornton Police received multiple calls from community members reporting they had seen Arebalo walking near Riverdale Road and 120th Avenue. Officers responded, and Arebalo was taken into custody without incident. He did not have any apparent injuries at the time of his arrest.

Formal charges will be determined by the 17th Judicial District Attorney’s Office.

On Oct. 11, at about 9:30 p.m., Thornton Police officers responded to the 12800 block of Ulster Street. During the incident, Arebalo fired multiple rounds at officers, striking one officer. A second officer returned fire. Arebalo fled the scene.

In the hours after the shooting, SWAT, K9 teams and patrol officers searched the area within the perimeter, supported by drones, a Denver Police Department helicopter and a Colorado State Patrol airplane.

Over the next two days, investigators searched Arebalo’s vehicle and the surrounding area, followed up on tips and worked with federal partners and neighboring jurisdictions to locate him. Arebalo’s name and photo were released to the public, and Metro Denver Crime Stoppers offered a reward of up to $4,000 for information leading to him.

The injured officer has been released from the hospital and is expected to make a full recovery.

We are grateful to the residents who recognized Arebalo and called 911. Those calls led directly to a safe arrest. Thank you also to Metro Denver Crime Stoppers and everyone in the community who shared his information over the past two days.

We are proud of the officers who responded that night and remained diligent under extremely dangerous circumstances. We are also proud of the investigators who worked around the clock to bring this to a safe end. Our dispatchers also played a critical role, managing a high volume of emergency calls, coordinating resources and keeping officers informed throughout.

Thornton Police Department is especially grateful to the agencies that assisted with K9 and area searches, perimeter support, air and drone support, SWAT and crisis negotiation, and handling calls for service in Thornton during the incident:

Adams County Sheriff’s Office
Arvada Police Department
Brighton Police Department
Broomfield Police Department
Colorado State Patrol
Commerce City Police Department
Denver Police Department
Federal Heights Police Department
Northglenn Police Department
RTD Transit Police
Westminster Police Department

This arrest is the result of our community and law enforcement working together, and we are grateful to everyone who played a part.

text:
ACC coaching hot seats: Norvell remains No. 1 as pressure rises at Clemson and NC State
*Rankings as of Oct. 11, 2026, incorporating games played through Oct. 10.*

Mike Norvell remains the ACC coach under the greatest pressure.** Florida State's commanding win over Virginia offered relief, but a 44-20 loss at Louisville renewed concerns about the Seminoles' direction. Meanwhile, Clemson's loss to Miami raises Dabo Swinney's position on this list, and North Carolina's victory at ranked Pitt gives Bill Belichick a meaningful boost.

***** All 17 ACC coaches, hottest seat to coolest *****

1. Mike Norvell - Florida State
Norvell has the clearest institutional demand for improvement. When Florida State retained him last November, its announcement explicitly called for changes to meet the program's championship standard. That followed consecutive losing seasons.
The Louisville game explains why he stays first. Florida State led 14-0, then lost by 24 while surrendering **397 rushing yards**. That performance undermined much of the reassurance supplied by the previous week's victory over Virginia.
What would help: Sustained conference success and evidence that FSU can handle adversity against strong opponents. The hottest seat does not necessarily mean an imminent dismissal.

2. Bill O'Brien - Boston College
Boston College's 2-10 finish in 2025 makes another disappointing season difficult to absorb. This year's Rutgers victory is a positive, but consecutive conference losses leave the Eagles needing a turnaround.
Expectations must remain realistic: BC was picked 16th in the preseason ACC poll. O'Brien needs to demonstrate meaningful progress against that modest baseline, rather than meet an invented championship requirement.
What would help: Conference victories, improved offensive consistency and a credible path toward bowl eligibility.

3. Dave Doeren - NC State
Doeren's position illustrates why the whole résumé matters. Beating Louisville 31-28 was valuable. Losing 38-14 to Wake Forest at home one week later substantially weakened the case that NC State had turned a corner.
The manner of the defeat matters: the Wolfpack led 14-10 at halftime, then were outscored **28-0 in the second half**. NC State finished with only 15 rushing yards. Those are substantial concerns about execution and the team's response as the game changed.
What would help: A strong second half of the season that builds on the Louisville win and avoids further decisive conference defeats.

4. Fran Brown - Syracuse
Syracuse's 3-9 season in 2025 places extra importance on Brown's third year. The Orange have opened conference play with three losses, although their narrow defeat at Virginia deserves more context than the record alone provides.
Syracuse led by 10 at halftime, and quarterback Malachi Nelson left late with an injury. Those circumstances temper the evaluation, but the need for conference wins remains.
What would help: Translating competitive performances into ACC victories and restoring a clear upward trajectory.

5. Dabo Swinney - Clemson
Swinney rises because Clemson has suffered two emphatic defeats in its biggest early tests: at LSU and at home against Miami. The Hurricanes' 41-13 victory is especially consequential for a program seeking to regain its standing within the conference.
His championship history provides substantial protection. That makes his situation different from Norvell's: mounting scrutiny of Clemson's direction does not establish that his job is immediately endangered.
What would help: A convincing ACC run and better performances against top opponents. Narrowing the gap with elite teams matters more than simply beating weaker opposition.

6. Bill Belichick - North Carolina
Belichick's seat cools after UNC won 21-17 at No. 25 Pitt, overcoming a 10-point deficit. It was Carolina's first ranked victory since 2023 and first ranked road victory since 2020.
After a 4-8 debut, that is tangible evidence of improvement. It does not settle the season, but it gives Belichick a stronger argument that his program is progressing.
What would help: Building on the Pitt win with consistent conference results and a postseason berth.

***** The remaining coaches *****

7. Brent Key, Georgia Tech.
The victory over previously unbeaten, nationally ranked Duke provides meaningful relief. Tech's own recap notes that Key improved to **8-1 against ranked ACC opponents**. The season still needs rescuing, but this win strengthens his case considerably.

8. Jeff Brohm, Louisville.
Louisville's preseason projection of third creates a substantial expectations gap at .500. However, its three defeats were each by three points, and the decisive win over Florida State supplied a strong response. Brohm faces performance pressure more than immediate job danger.

9. Tony Elliott, Virginia.
Last year's 11-3 season affords Elliott considerable standing. The defeat at Florida State raised questions, but beating Syracuse prevented consecutive losses. His position remains comparatively secure.

10. Pat Narduzzi, Pitt.
Losing at home to UNC hurts, particularly after an unbeaten start. Nevertheless, five wins and a road victory at Virginia Tech make a strong current case for security. The remaining season will determine whether Pitt sustains that progress.

11. Tavita Pritchard, Stanford.
Consecutive heavy defeats to Wake Forest and Notre Dame increase scrutiny of the rebuild. As a first-year coach at the program picked last in the ACC, Pritchard should still have substantial time to develop it. His higher position reflects concern about results, not evidence of imminent removal.

12. Tosh Lupoi, California.
Beating Virginia Tech helps the first-year coach's position after the loss at UNLV. Cal has a winning conference record, and its early results offer a reasonable foundation for a new tenure.

13. James Franklin, Virginia Tech.
Consecutive defeats to Pitt and Cal interrupted the unbeaten start. They raise competitive questions, but Franklin remains early in his first season and has already produced four victories. His job appears secure.

14. Rhett Lashlee, SMU.
The Mustangs remain well positioned after last year's nine-win season. Expectations are high, but the current record supports confidence rather than a serious hot-seat argument.

15. Manny Diaz, Duke.
One close road loss does little to erase the security earned by a defending ACC champion with a strong start. Diaz faces the challenge of keeping Duke in contention; his job-security risk remains low.

16. Jake Dickert, Wake Forest.
The victory in Raleigh strengthens an already impressive second season. Dickert has Wake substantially outperforming its preseason projection of 13th, following a nine-win debut. His seat is among the coolest in the league.

17. Mario Cristobal, Miami.
The preseason conference favorite remains unbeaten and has delivered an emphatic road win at Clemson. Championship expectations are substantial, but Miami's results and trajectory give Cristobal the strongest security case in the ACC.

[These are editorial assessments of job security, based on results, opponent strength, recent program trajectory, coaching tenure and expectations. They do not establish that administrators have decided to make changes. The lower half of the list contains coaches whose jobs appear relatively secure.]

Big modded colonies that crawl at max speed are the ones to test on the beta. Early players report much higher frame rates but 12 to 13 GB of RAM used at startup, so check your memory before.

If you own anything there, download and back up the installers before February 28. Prime Gaming's October 22 drop includes a Legacy Games code, so redeem and download that one fast too.

• Duke Nukem 3D Level Designer Richard 'Levelord' Gray Has Died
If you play boomer shooters or make maps for them, a lot of the secret-room and set-piece design you enjoy traces back to him. Fire up a Duke level tonight and find his room.

Hello, I am Palestinian. 
And since honesty is rare in my politics, let me admit a few things.
1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised the war would “throw the Jews into the sea.” Instead, I lost everything and it was called the Nakba. Not because I was not offered a state, but because I rejected it.
1948–2025. The Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they kept me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and cages for me. They used me as propaganda, not as a human being.
1967. After another war I lost, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on “no peace, no recognition, no negotiations.” Three no’s. Fifty years later, I am still without a state. It turns out rejection does not pay the rent.
Oslo, the 1990s. Israel said: “Let’s try.” It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions of dollars in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an Intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

text:
Location 1: Turquzabad

Information available to the IAEA suggests that Iran used the Turquzabad site, previously referred to in agency reports as Location 1, to store nuclear material and equipment, including containers transferred from Varamin (location 3). In January 2019, the IAEA requested that Iran clarify whether the site was used for such purposes. Iran told the IAEA there were no undeclared materials or activities at the location. In February 2019, IAEA inspectors then requested information from Iran about the movement of containers from the site that the agency observed using satellite imagery and requested access to the location. Environmental samples taken indicated the presence of processed uranium.

Iran’s initial responses to the IAEA regarding the presence of the processed uranium were not deemed technically credible. As a result of the March 2022 agreement between the IAEA and Iran, Tehran provided further explanation for the presence of the uranium, saying that there was “the possibility of an act of sabotage by a third party to contaminate the area.” Iran provided no evidence to support that claim, according to the May 2022 IAEA report. Iran also said it could not identify where containers removed from site in 2018 are currently located.

Iran and the IAEA exchanged letters regarding Turquzabad in 2023. In August 2023, Iran told the IAEA that none of the storage containers removed from the site were intact; all were dismantled at the location. Iran did say it could provide the IAEA with information regarding the current location of the dismantled containers.

As of November 2024, Iran had not provided any additional information about the containers and IAEA report concluded that the presence of uranium particles at the site “is not clarified.”

Location 2: Lavisan-Shian

The IAEA investigated evidence of an undeclared uranium metal disc that had undergone drilling and processing at Lavisan-Shian, previously identified as Location 2. As part of its investigation, the IAEA visited a declared facility in Iran where uranium metal discs had been produced but was unable to determine if the Lavisan-Shian disc was at that site. The IAEA informed Iran in January 2022 that it “could not exclude that the disc had been melted, recast and was not part of the declared nuclear material inventory.” In its May 2022 report, the IAEA assessed that the activities at Lavisan-Shian “were not declared by Iran to the Agency as required under the Safeguards Agreement.” The IAEA also said it has no further questions about this location.

Location 3: Varamin

Information and evidence available to the IAEA suggests that Iran used Varamin for storing nuclear materials and/or fuel-cycle-related activities. The IAEA’s evidence suggests that materials and equipment from the site were moved to Location 1, Turquazabad, for storage.

The IAEA requested access to Varamin in January 2020, but Tehran denied the request. Inspectors were able to access the site after Iran and the agency reached an agreement in August 2020 and environmental samples confirmed the presence of uranium at the location. The IAEA ask Iran to provide clarifications about the presence of uranium, which Tehran has failed to credibly answer.

In the May 2022 report, the IAEA noted that Iran stated in March 2022 that the location was used for the production of sodium sulphate. The IAEA stated that this explanation does not match the satellite imagery taken from the site and the results of the environmental samples that were collected during an August 2020 visit to the site. Furthermore, it does not explain the presence of the uranium particles. The IAEA reported that Iran offered the additional explanation of third-party sabotage to contaminate the area but provided no evidence to support that claim. In the report, the IAEA offers its assessment of Varamin, that it was an “undeclared pilot-scale facility for the processing and milling of uranium ore and conversion into uranium oxide” and possible UF4 and UF6 at laboratory scale from 1999-2003.

As of November 2024, the IAEA has received no credible explanations for the presence of uranium at Varamin and its investigation of the site remains open.

Location 4: Marivan

Informational available to the IAEA suggests that Iran intended to use nuclear materials at Marivan. The IAEA reported that safeguards relevant information suggests that Iran conducted “explosive experiments with protective shielding in preparation for the use of neutron detectors” at one of the areas under investigation at Marivan, previously referred to as Location 4 by the IAEA.

The IAEA requested access to the site in January 2020, which Tehran denied. Inspectors were later able to visit the location and take environmental samples as part of the August 2020 agreement between the agency and Iran. In January 2021, the IAEA requested clarification from Iran regarding the presence of processed uranium found at the site.

In August 2021, Iran provided the agency with some documentation about Marivan and said that one of the areas in question was built to support a mine managed by another IAEA member state until it was abandoned in 1994 and that the bunkers at the site were used for deactivating munitions. The IAEA assessed that some of this documentation was inconsistent with its evidence. As part of the process initiated by the March 2022 process, Iran informed the IAEA that it had never produced the type of material found at the site and that the presence might be accounted for by an act of third-party sabotage to contaminate the site. Iran, however, provided no evidence for this claim. During the consultations, Iran also said that some of the photographs of the bunkers were fabricated.

The IAEA and Iran conducted additional exchanges about Marivan in 2023. Iran maintained its previous claim that a third-party state operating a mine and chemical lab at the site contaminated the area with uranium and provided additional information about the lab.The IAEA said this was a "possible" explanation for the presence of uranium at the site. In a May 2023 report, the IAEA said it had no further questions regarding Marivan.

Iranian Safeguards Noncompliance (2025)

Overview

In February 2021, Iran suspended the implementation of the monitoring mechanism included in the JCPOA that were not legally required by the NPT. This included the additional protocol to its safeguards agreement and other specific provisions that expanded IAEA access and monitoring mechanisms, such as the requirement for daily access to Natanz and Fordow enrichment facilties.

As part of the February 2021 suspension, Iran said it would no longer implement Modified Code 3.1 to its safeguards agreement. Modified Code 3.1 requires that a state provide information to the IAEA about new nuclear facilities when a decision is made to construct a new nuclear facility, or construction begins (whichever is sooner). The original Code 3.1 only required notification to the IAEA 180 days before the introduction of nuclear materials. The decision to modify Code 3.1 gives the IAEA a longer time period to design an effective safeguards approach.

The IAEA and the IAEA's Board of Governors maintain that Iran cannot unilaterally modify or suspend Modified Code 3.1. After the IAEA reported that Iran was constructing new nuclear facilities but had not provided the necessary design information to the IAEA in accordance with the Modified Code 3.1, the IAEA's Board of Governors passed two resolutions in 2024 that included provisions calling upon Iran to implement Modified Code 3.1.

In June 2025, the IAEA Board of Governors passed a resolution finding Iran in noncompliance with its safeguards agreement. The resolution mentioned Iran's failure to implement Modified Code 3.1 and its failure to cooperate with the IAEA on the 2018 investigation into the presence of nuclear materials found at undeclared locations (see above).

In November 2025, the IAEA Board passed another resolution reiterating that Iran must meet its NPT-required safeguards obligations. That resolution followed a November IAEA report that assessed that the agency lost its continuity of knowledge regarding Iran's stockpiles of nuclear materials. Iran's decision to suspend IAEA access to sites bombed by Israel and the United States during the 12-day war (June 2025) and not to provide the IAEA with updated nuclear material accountancy reports led to the agency's determination.

text:
Short Notes On: Future Trends And Violence

Clear view: As states become less able or willing to guarantee security, Private Military Companies may increasingly become providers of coercive capacity. And the supply of people, expertise and technology capable of providing that security could grow significantly following the war in Ukraine.

1. Erik Prince is most famous for running Blackwater, a PMC deployed extensively in the War on Terror. The firm’s behaviour in some incidents drew extremely valid criticism, most famously the Nisour Square massacre. He now runs Vectus Global, which is deployed in the below vid and in DRC.

2. This among other reasons has largely turned respectable commentators off the idea of PMCs. Our current commentators are not alone in this - Machiavelli was not a fan either, and unsurprisingly the Chinese Communist Party doesn’t like PMCs either. They have a long and interesting history which is poorly understood in contemporary Western politics. 

3. However, I think it’s worth thinking about what PMCs - or their security counterparts, PSCs, which are different - may offer in a future where three things happen at once. 

—> Countries become more transactional and less assured of US or allied military support
—> Loads of highly trained young men emerge from the wreckage of the Ukraine war seeking new opportunities
—> commodities and raw goods need protection (ranging from fishing stocks to data centres)

4. It is through this prism that I tend to view Prince’s ongoing work in Haiti. This is a Petri Dish for seeing how western PMCs can become the reinforcement arm for a state that has lost monopoly on power. The Russians have done this for some time with Wagner, now Africa Corp, with varying levels of success (and mixed loyalties).

5. So while I don’t expect anyone who doesn’t like the idea of PMCs being utilised from a moral POV (totally fine btw) to change their mind, I would just note that we will probably see in the next few years a huge number of highly trained young men from countries like Ukraine and Columbia enter the market looking for work. 

6. As I’ve argued for before, Britain could pre-empt some of this AND make money by building or supporting a British counterpart working on two specific issues: illegal fishing in the Commonwealth, and data centre protection (this one feels intuitive but need to think harder.) 

7. One final note: this may feel like a conversation that sits outside the Overton Window, but back in 2002, Foreign Sec Jack Straw presented a white paper pondering if Britain should think more clearly about regulating this sector.

No other human being comes close to this!

Tell me, what false prophet would stand in prayer as an obligation for six hours almost every night, then perform many more prayers during the day ON TOP of the five daily prayers? These were prayers that only he was obligated to perform by God. We are not expected to do them because we don’t have the ability to, as Allah gave him the strength to do so. What false prophet would continuously fast outside the month of Ramadan, going many days without breaking his fast? What kind of man would do this if he wanted convenience, power, and wealth? What human being had the ability, stamina, and strength to do all this besides a prophet of God?

He would feed 70 people a day, twice a day. All the while, he was teaching and lecturing on Islam and the Quran, providing guidance and counseling on marriage and social issues, issuing rulings as a judge and governor of a state, and serving as an arbiter. He was essentially a psychological and spiritual counselor, arguably the greatest military commander and warrior in history, a husband, a father, and a nephew. He married older women who were widows of war and had children, helping protect them from financial and housing insecurity, while also strengthening tribal alliances by marrying women from different tribes as a political strategy. What human being in history do you know who had the wisdom, genius, stamina, strength, patience, and tolerance to do all these things, day and night? No human being could do all this without direct help, guidance, and strength from God!

The tribes of Makkah offered him money, power, wealth, women, and status in exchange for stopping his preaching of Islam. He told them that even if they placed the sun in his right hand and the moon in his left, he would never stop, by Allah! What false prophet, grifter, or conman behaves like this? He turned down power, wealth, money, women, and status. This completely undermines the claim that he was a false prophet, grifter, or conman because it makes no sense to think someone seeking those things would behave this way.

Prophet Muhammad died without leaving behind money or wealth for his family to inherit. He was a Messenger of God, and no special privileges were to be given to his family. That’s why none of his sons survived: they all died in infancy or childhood, preventing any direct male successor to him. That’s also why he never named any of his cousins, such as Ali, or his nephews, Hasan or Husayn, as his successor. In Islam, lineage plays no role in religious authority, and he didn’t want to give anyone the impression that his family had special rights or privileges. There are many examples of this throughout his life, when he could have treated his family differently in matters of rulings and justice, but he didn’t.

His mother and father died before he was eight years old. He lost his beloved first wife, Khadijah, along with his grandfather and uncle, within a relatively short period. He lost nearly all his children during his lifetime; all but one died before him, and that daughter died a few months after him. His life was marked by pain and tragedy, as were the lives of the other prophets of God!

Allah gave him the choice to be a prophet-king like Solomon, but he chose the life of a poor and simple prophet to identify with the poor and needy. What human being do you know in history who was this humble? He used to sit on the floor, blending in with his companions. When important delegates from other states came to meet him, his companions sometimes had to point him out because he would sit among them, and they wouldn’t immediately know which one was the Prophet.

The Bible is not the infallible record of God's dealings with humanity, as its own tradition suggests. It is a collection of texts written by human hands over centuries, and the anachronisms it contains betray composition dates far later than the eras they claim to narrate. There are dozens of reasons to say so, but two fronts are enough: the book of Isaiah and the Pentateuch.

1. Isaiah: a prophet who "predicts" what has already happened

Isaiah 1-39 is set in the eighth century BC, in the time of Hezekiah and the Assyrian threat. But from chapter 40 onward the text enters a different world: it speaks of a Jerusalem already destroyed, a people exiled in Babylon, and their comfort drawing near (Isa 40:1-2). And in Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1, a Persian king named Cyrus appears as God's shepherd and anointed one, roughly 150 years before he was born.

This is the timestamp the author could not erase. Genuine biblical prophecy tends to speak in general terms; this text names a king, describes the fall of Babylon as imminent (Isa 46-47), and addresses exiles living under Babylonian rule, not Assyrian. The vocabulary, style, and theology (strict, explicit monotheism and mockery of Babylonian idols) match the mid-sixth century BC. This is why critical scholarship, from Doederlein and Duhm onward, concludes that an anonymous "Deutero-Isaiah" wrote during the exile. A prophet living in 700 BC would not address an audience that did not yet exist as though it were already in captivity.

2. The Pentateuch: Moses writing about his own death and about things that did not yet exist

Tradition attributes the first five books to Moses, around the fifteenth or thirteenth century BC. But the text is full of anachronisms:

Deuteronomy 34 narrates the death and burial of Moses, and says that "there arose no prophet since in Israel like unto Moses," a sentence that could only be written long afterward.
Genesis 36:31 lists "the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel." The writer knows Israel already had kings, something that happens centuries after Moses.
Genesis 11:28-31 and 15:7 speak of "Ur of the Chaldees." The Chaldeans do not appear as a significant group in Mesopotamia until the early first millennium BC, long after the patriarchal age.
Domesticated camels in the stories of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Gen 12:16, 24) are anachronistic: the archaeological evidence indicates they were widely used as pack animals only around the tenth century BC or later.
The Philistines appear in the days of Abraham and Isaac (Gen 21:32-34; 26), but they arrived on the Canaanite coast with the Sea Peoples, around 1175 BC.
Genesis 14:14 says Abraham pursued his enemies "unto Dan," but that city received the name in the period of the judges (Judg 18:29), centuries later.
Exodus 1:11 mentions the cities of Pithom and Raamses. The reference fits first-millennium Egypt better than the age of the patriarchs.
Numbers 12:3 declares that Moses was "very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth," hard to accept as the author's self-praise.
Genesis 12:6, "the Canaanite was then in the land," implies a narrator for whom the Canaanites were no longer there.

3. Egypt and the Exodus: an escape that left no trace

Exodus speaks of 600,000 adult men, implying around two million people, who crossed the Sinai and wandered for forty years. Not a single excavation in the Sinai has found traces of a camp of that size, even though archaeology has found remains of much smaller and older groups. The Egyptians, meticulous record-keepers, mention neither the ten plagues, nor the death of the firstborn, nor the loss of a pharaonic army in the sea. Nor is there archaeological evidence of a violent conquest of Canaan like the one described in Joshua: cities such as Jericho and Ai, according to excavations, were uninhabited or did not exist in the proposed period.

4. The flood: an ancient myth with a biblical name

The story of Noah repeats almost point for point that of Utnapishtim in the Epic of Gilgamesh and that of Atrahasis, much older Mesopotamian texts: a god decides to destroy humanity, a righteous man is ordered to build a boat, he carries animals, and at the end he sends out birds to learn whether the waters have receded and offers a sacrifice. A global flood covering the highest mountains about 4,500 years ago is incompatible with geology, and no stratum records it. The logistics are also impossible: eight people caring for millions of animal species on a wooden vessel, with no neighboring people (Egyptians, Sumerians, Chinese) noticing that their civilization was wiped out and restarted.

5. Two stories stitched together and an impossible authorship

The text itself shows its seams. Genesis contains two creation accounts that do not agree on the order of events (Gen 1 and 2), two flood accounts interwoven with contradictory details (two of each animal, or seven pairs of the clean? Gen 6:19 and 7:2), two different names for God in separate blocks, and two versions of a patriarch presenting his wife as his sister before a king. This is what the documentary hypothesis, with its J, E, P, and D sources, explains naturally: several texts from different periods were sewn together by editors, probably during or after the Babylonian exile.

Conclusion

These texts contradict history and one another because they were not written by the eyewitnesses they claim to be, but by later scribes who projected their own world onto an idealized past. When verifiable details fail again and again, the narrative stops being testimony and becomes a devotional construction.

I do not claim to know whether a god exists. I am an agnostic, which means I do not pretend to that certainty. What I do maintain is that a book presented as inspired and infallible should pass the most basic test: agreeing with itself and with history.

Believers, I invite you to investigate this calmly, reading the full texts and consulting independent sources, without relying solely on what your pastor or your tradition has told you must be concluded. If your faith is sound, it will withstand the questions.

May everyone think for themselves.

"Our Affairs are at present in a most delicate, tho' I hope a fortunate Situation: But the great and radical Evil which pervades our whole System and like an Ax at the Tree of our Safety, Interest and Liberty here again shews its hateful Influence. Tomorrow the Continental Troops are all at Liberty. I wish to push our Success to keep up the Pannick and in order to get their Assistance have promised them a Bounty of 10 Dollars if they will continue for one Month. But here again a new Difficulty presents itself we have not Money to pay the Bounty, and we have exhausted our Credit by such frequent Promises that it has not the Weight we could wish. If it be possible, Sir, to give us Assistance do it; borrow Money where it can be done we are doing it upon our private Credit; every Man of Interest and every Lover of his Country must strain his Credit upon such an Occasion. No Time my dear Sir is to be lost." George Washington, Letter to Robert Morris, Head Quarters, Trenton, December 31, 1776

Source: https://t.co/yZwUV1r2wk

What can we learn?

Written just days after the surprise victory at the Battle of Trenton, George Washington wanted to strike the British again while they were panicking, but his army was about to dissolve. The enlistment contracts for the vast majority of Washington's troops expired at midnight on January 1, 1777. Legally, the soldiers were free to go home, leaving Washington with almost no army. To convince the troops to stay for one more month, Washington promised them a $10 bounty. 

As a backdrop, the Continental Congress had authorized $5 million in paper currency to pay military bonuses, but its credit had deteriorated so severely that many citizens refused to accept it as payment(1). Washington faced a critical shortage of funds and appealed to Robert Morris, Pennsylvania’s master of finance, to secure hard currency(2).

The stakes were extraordinarily high. By December 1776, Washington’s Continental Army was shrinking as soldier enlistments expired(2). Without payment in actual coin, his soldiers would not extend their service into the new year(2). Morris understood that pursuing the British after the Trenton victory offered the only realistic opportunity to sustain the revolutionary cause; failure to capitalize on this momentum would likely result in its collapse(3).

Morris responded with remarkable resourcefulness. Initially doubting his ability to raise the sum, Morris left his office in a despondent state and encountered a wealthy Quaker member while walking home(*1). When the Quaker asked what security Morris could offer, he replied “My note and my honor,” and the Quaker immediately agreed, with Morris dispatching $50,000 to Washington the following day(1).

With soldiers paid in hard money, enough of Washington’s ragged forces agreed to continue their service(2). This enabled the victories at Trenton and Princeton that proved pivotal to sustaining the Revolution. Historians have observed that without Morris’s fundraising efforts, the Revolution’s success would have been virtually impossible(3). Morris’s willingness to stake his personal reputation and credit—rather than relying on worthless government currency—transformed a moment of potential collapse into a turning point for American independence.

1. Benson Lossing, ed., Harper’s Encyclopedia of United States History (Medford, MA: Perseus Digital Library, n.d.).
2. William J. Bennett, America: The Last Best Hope (Volume I): From the Age of Discovery to a World at War (Nashville, TN: Thomas Nelson, 2007).
3. Michael Tait with TobyMac, Under God (Bethany House, 2004).

text:
WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

ORLANDO FURIOSO VI

Pietro studied the map. Aldo marked the roads. Adelaide laid out the accounts, showing how long our stores would last if the routes were closed. Bernat, who had retourned with a company of Catalans willing to serve for a further month, asked whether we intended to fight.

“We shall have to,” I said.

“Where?”

“Not where he expects.”

Pietro smiled faintlie.

The Hegemon had men, horses, and money. He had also a great road which consumed the treasurie, allies who were beginning to doubt him, and a network of supporters whose loyalté depended upon their expectatioun of profit. We had fewer men, less money, and no secure territorie. But we knew the countrie, and we had the goodwill of people who could tell us where the soldatos were going before the soldatos themselves knew.

We would not attempt to defend everie villauge. We would not gather in one place and allow Herod to surround us. We would move between the roads, strike at the wagons carrieing supplies, and force his men to divide their strength. We would make him pay for everie mile of countrieside he sought to control.

It was not a grand plan. It was the onlie one we could afford.

As the council ended, Emiglio leaned over the map.

“Thou knowest,” he said, “if we keep taking his wagons, the Hegemon may eventuallie run out of wagons.”

“An excellent observatioun.”

“And then?”

“Then he may have to build another road.”

Emiglio grinned.

For the fyrst time in many weeks, I laughed without effort.

I have been asked since whether I believed I could defeat Herod Malvezzi.

The questioun is usuallie put by men who wish to know whether I was brave, or foolish, or possessed of some rare gyft of foresight. They would prefer to believe that I saw the end from the beginning, that I understood the whole shape of the conflict, and that everie actioun was part of a design which had been clear in my mind from the fyrst.

It was not so.

I was a merchaunt whose goods had been taken, a man whose appeal to the law had failed, and a husband who had learned that the safeté of his familie myght depend upon the speed of a horse and the kindnesse of a neighbour. I had gathered men because I needed them, and they had remained because they needed me. I had taken money from the Hegemon’s supporters because they had profited from his rule, and I had given some of it away because the people who had helped me were not all soldatos.

I had won a battle because we had chosen the ground, because Pietro’s archers had kept their heads, because Bernat’s Catalans were skylled, and because Ser Niccolò had mistaken his fyne armour for a plan. I had captured a Malvezzi because the Hegemon’s men had been badlie arranged upon a narrow road. I had escaped the worst of Herod’s reprisals because two riders had reached my familie in time.

There was no miracle in it.

There was work, and luck, and a number of men who had been willing to trust one another for a little longer than seemed reasonable.

The Hegemon remained powerful. His road continued. His allies still held offices, estates, and contracts. His soldatos still rode through Bologne, and his clerks still entered sums in books which few men were permitted to examine. The factiouns of Emilia continued to calculate what myght be gayned from our quarrel. Some offered help; others prepared to oppose us; many waited to see which side would prove more profitable.

I had not liberated Bologne. I had not restored everie stolen house, freed everie prisoner, or payd everie debt. I had not even recovered all my own goods.

But the Hegemon had been forced to bargayn. His cousin had been held for ransom. His supporters had begun to questioun the pryce of their allegiaunce. Men who had once feared to speak his name in anger now repeated my letter in taverns and workshops, laughing at the jester and asking why the One Way cost so much while their own streets remained broken.

The laughter was dangereux. It did not overthrow a ruler, but it loosened something in the minds of those who had believed his authorité beyond questioun.

I had become, without intending it, a man to whom others brought their grievaunces. Some came because they believed I could help them. Some because they wished to profit from my quarrel. Some because they hated Herod more than they trusted me. I accepted their serwyce when it was useful, refused their demaunds when they threatened to corrupt the company, and tried to remember that the men who followed me were not pieces upon a boaurd.

I had begun this enterpryse seeking repyment.

Now I found myself responsible for men who had no goods to recover, no contract to enforce, and no hope of retourning to the lives they had once known. Their homes had been demolished. Their trades had been destroyed. Their families had been taken. They had come to me because Herod had made the cité unlivable, and because the countrieside offered them at least the possibilité of beginning agayn.

I could not send them all home.

Nor could I promise them that the world would be kinder when Herod was gone.

That was the danger of becoming a cause. Men myght begin by following thee for what thou canst give them, and end by expecting thee to become the answer to everie injurie they have suffered. A captain may be a man, but a cause is an appetite. It grows with everie victorie, and it is ne'er satisfied.

I would have to learn how to lead without allowing the cause to devour those who had made it possible.

That evening I walked beyond the camp, where the trees thinned and the road descended towaurds the plain. From the ridge I could see the distant lights of Bologne, and farther off, the pale line of the One Way where the unfynished stone caught the last light of the sky.

The road had cost the cité a fortune. It had displaced households, ruined trades, and enriched men who had ne'er lifted a hammer. It was meant to bear the Hegemon’s name into posterité, to show future generatiouns that one man had possessed the wealth and will to alter the shape of a cité.

I wondered what those future generatiouns would see.

Perhaps they would admire the road. Perhaps they would curse it. Perhaps the stones would remain long after Herod’s House had fallen, and men would walk upon them without knowing whose houses had been torn down to make room.

A road is a curious monument. It belongs to the man who pays for it onlie until it is fynished. After that, it belongs to everieone who uses it.

I thought of my father, who had taught me to reckon the value of a thing by what it cost and what it retourned. He had not taught me that a man myght spend his whole fortune upon a work whose greatest retourn was the suffering of others. Nor had he taught me what to do when the man responsible for such a work could not be brought before a court.

I had learned those things from Herod.

The wind rose, moving through the trees. Somewhere behind me, a sentrie called to another, and a horse stamped in the yaurd. I could hear the company settling for the nyght: the clatter of bowls, the low voices of men, the scrape of a chair upon the ground. They were not an army fit to conquer Emilia. They were a collectioun of people who had been cheated, driven out, or abandoned, and who had decided that they would not endure their misfortunes in silence.

I had once believed that the world was held together by contracts.

I now knew that contracts were onlie as strong as the men who enforced them, and that the men who enforced them were often the verie men who profited by their breaking.

Yet I had not abandoned the ledger. I still counted the wauges, entered the debts, and recorded the names of those who had suffered. I still believed that a man should know what he owed and what was owed to him. If that was a small principle upon which to build a war, it was the onlie one I possessed.

I retourned to the camp and found Adelaide waiting beside the table.

She had prepared the accounts for the coming month. The figures were not encouraging. We had money enough to sustain the company for a time, but not enough to fight a prolonged campaign without further income. The Catalans would require their wauges. The horses would need fodder. The wounded would need care. The families who had lost their households would need help.

I studied the columns.

“How much?” I asked.

She told me.

I nodded.

“Then we shall have to earn it.”

She closed the book. “And if we cannot?”

I thought of the road, the prisoners, the men who had left us, and the letters from the factiouns. I thought of Herod in his palays, surrounded by counsellors who assured him that the cité’s suffering was the pryce of greatnesse.

“Then we shall have to choose what we can afford to lose.”

Adelaide looked at me for a long moment, then opened the book agayn.

Outside, the sentries changed wautch. The fire burned low. The men slept beneath their blankets, some with weapons beside them, others with their honds curled beneath their heads like childeren. Tomorrow we would send scouts towaurds Bologne. We would learn which roads remained open, which Houses had committed themselves to the Hegemon, and which of his supporters had begun to look for another maister. We would seek new allies, though we would not surrender our independence to them. We would gather the men who had been driven from the cité, and we would give them work where work could be found.

And when Herod sent his soldatos, as he surelie would, we would meet them on ground of our choosing.

I had no great prophecy to offer my company. I could not tell them that we would win, or that their families would be restored, or that Bologne would one day be governed by men who understood the pryce of a loaf of bread. I could not promise that our cause would remain pure, or that I would always judge ryghtlie.

I could onlie promise that I would keep the accounts.

The Hegemon had his title, his palays, his counsellors, his road, and the great machinerie of a cité arranged to serve him. He had spent gulden by the cartload to make himself immortal, and had made enemies by the household.

I had men who remembered the account.

And the account was not settled.

The thorn remained. And the flesh had begun to bleed.

text:
WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

ORLANDO FURIOSO III

At dawn, we took our places.

The convoy came later than expected.

The fyrst sound was the creaking of wheels, slow and uneven, followed by the clatter of harnesse and the voices of men urging tired horses onwaurd. Mist lay over the stream. The alder branches were bare, and the grass upon the bank was sylvered with frost. From the slope, Pietro’s archers wautched the road without speaking.

Fourteen wagons emerged between the trees.

The fyrst carried grain. The second carried grain. The third carried iron beneath a canvas cover, and the fourth grain agayn. The guaurds rode in pairs along the sides, with two men at the front and three at the rear. Their captain rode near the middle, beneath a small banner bearing the Malvezzi arms. He wore a helmet polished bryght enough to cautch the morning light.

Ser Niccolò himself was not difficult to recognise. His horse was too fyne for the road, and his armour bore a gilded border which would have been better suited to a tournament. He rode with the loose, careless posture of a man who believed that the world had been arranged for his convenience.

I waited until the fyrst wagons entered the ford.

Then I raised my hond.

Pietro’s archers loosed upon the road ahead of the convoy. Their arrows struck the ground before the lead horses, and one guaurd’s mount reared so violentlie that the man was thrown into the stream. At the same moment, Aldo’s men emerged from the trees beyond the crossing, blocking the road with a felled branch and a cartwheel. The wagons halted. The guaurds shouted. The horses pressed agaynst one another, and the drivers began to curse.

I gave the signal for Bernat.

The Catalans came out from behind the bend at a run.

They did not crie out as they charged. They moved in a haurd, disciplined line, their shields close, their weapons held low. The fyrst guaurds tried to form a defence beside the wagons, but the ground was too narrow and the horses too fryghtened. A man fell beneath a wheel. Another was struck from his saddle. The rest tourned towaurds the Catalans, who struck them before they could settle.

I had thought myself prepared for the noise of battle. I was not.

Steel upon steel is a sharp sound, but the sounds around it are worse: the scream of a horse, the grunt of a man struck in the bellie, the sudden, astonished crie of someone who has discovered that his body is not as strong as he believed. There is no music in it, and no dignité. Men stumble in the mud. They lose their footing. They call for their mothers. They trie to ryse with wounds that will not permit them to stand.

I had brought men into this place to win a victorie. For a moment, as the fyrst struggle began, I wished onlie that it myght end.

Then Ser Niccolò rallied his guaurds.

He was no cowaurd. I give him that. He rode into the confusioun with his swerd drawn, shouting for his men to close ranks. Two of them followed him; a third seized the reins of a riderless horse and forced it out of the crush. The guaurds began to gather beside the wagons, using the wheels as cover. They were not well trained, but they had numbers, and the Catalans were now fighting upon ground where they could not easilie tourn.

I saw Bernat take a blow upon his shield and answer with a thrust that drove his opponent backwaurds into the stream. I saw Pietro’s archers loose agayn, not at the men themselves but at the horses behind them, whose panic would break the line. I saw Aldo drag one of our men out from beneath a fallen animal, then tourn and strike a guaurd who had come too close.

I also saw that the rear of the convoy was moving.

The empté wagon was not empté. Its canvas had slipped, revealing chests bound in iron. The guaurds were attempting to draw it back along the road, where a small escort had remained out of the fyrst struggle. If they escaped with the money, the battle myght yet become a costlie failure. We could seize the grain and iron, but we would be unable to pay the Catalans, and our victorie would be a tale told by hungrie men.

I took six riders and went after them.

The road beyond the ford was narrow, and the wagons had left deep ruts in the mud. We could not charge at full speed. I rode beside the ditch, shouting for the drivers to stop, and one of the guaurds tourned and fired a crossbow at me. The bolt passed so close to my face that I heaurd it before I saw it strike the tree behind me.

I confess that I swore.

The guaurd began to reload. I urged my horse forwaurd, caught the bridle of the nearest wagon, and hauled it sideways. The wheels struck the bank. The driver cried out. The wagon lurched, and the guaurd who had been standing beside it fell beneath the axle.

The others drew their swerds.

I had no great skyll with a swerd. I had learned enough to keep from being killed by a man who was not much better than I, and little more. My weapon caught upon a guaurd’s shield. He struck me across the shoulder, and pain flashed down my arm. I stumbled agaynst the wagon, felt the edge of his blade pass my cheek, and thought, with remarkable clarité, that I had made a poore bargayn indeed.

Then Emiglio appeared beside me with a pole from the wagon’s own frame and struck the guaurd behind the knee. The man fell. One of my riders seized his swerd, and another dragged him clear.

I found myself breathing haurd, my left hond numb, my mouth full of the taste of blood. I had bitten my tongue.

“Are the chests worth this?” Emiglio asked.

“I hope so.”

“Thou myght have asked them to surrender.”

“I did.”

“Perhaps thou shouldst ask more loudlie.”

I looked at the remaining guaurds. They had seen their captain’s line break, their wagon overtourn, and their companiouns fall. One threw down his swerd. Another followed. The third hesitated until Emiglio raised the pole agayn.

“Enough,” I said.

We took the chests.

By the time we retourned to the ford, the battle was nearlie fynished. Ser Niccolò had been unhorsed and was fighting on foot beside the largest wagon. Two men had been wounded trieing to reach him; the rest of his guaurds were beginning to give ground. Bernat’s Catalans pressed them steadilie, while Pietro’s archers held the road beyond.

I rode into the clearing and shouted that any man who laid down his weapon would be spared.

Some did so at once. Others continued to fight. One guaurd, a tall fellawe with a red beaurd, charged me with his swerd raised above his head. I tourned my horse aside and struck at him with the flat of my blade. He stumbled, and Aldo’s men took him.

Ser Niccolò saw that the battle was lost. He looked towaurds the trees, then at the wagons, then at the men who had fallen around him. He myght have escaped. Instead, he called for his remaining guaurds to stand down.

It was a brave decisioun, though perhaps not a wise one.

When he surrendered, I ordered that his wounds be bound. He had a cut across his forehead and a broken fynger. His armour was scrautched, his fyne cloak torn, and his gilded helmet had been trampled into the mud. He looked at me with a hatred so pure that I almost admired it.

“You have made an enemy of the House Malvezzi,” he said.

“I had done so before breakfast.”

“Herod will destroy you.”

“Then I shall endeavour not to be here when he arrives.”

He spat at my feet.

I let him.

The battle had lasted less than an hour. We had lost four men, two of whom were dead before the sun reached its height. Nine others were wounded. Bernat had taken a cut across the arm; Pietro had a broken bow and a bruised shoulder; Emiglio had escaped injurie, though he insisted that his pole had been the true hero of the day.

The enemy had lost more. Some had been killed, some wounded, and many had surrendered. We had captured the wagons, the grain, the iron, the horses, and the chests. We had also taken Ser Niccolò Malvezzi, cousin to the Hegemon, and a man whose ransom myght be worth more than everiething else combined.

We buried the dead before we counted the booté.

I had learned that much from my father, who had been a merchaunt and a decent man, though neither his decency nor his trade had protected him from death. A dead man cannot pay his debts, and a living man who believes his captain will leave him in the mud is unlikelie to follow that captain into the next fight.

When the graves were covered, we gathered the prisoners in the lee of the road and brought out the chests.

There were more gulden than I had dared hope.

I counted them twyce. Adelaide counted them a third time, and then informed me that the sum was smaller than the factour’s contract had declared. The difference was not great, but it was enough to prove that someone had been stealing from the convoy before we arrived.

I laughed.

Even in defeat, the Hegemon’s servaunts had managed to rob themselves.

Bernat demaunded his share. I payd the agreed sum, the cost of the passauge, and the promised portioun of the booté. The Catalans took their money without ceremony. One of them examined the horses, chose the best, and announced that the beast had a poore mouth. Another asked whether the iron could be sold in Ferrara. A third sat upon a wagon and ate an apple.

I had imagined that victorie would feel like triumph.

Instead, I was tired, sore, and afraid of what would follow.

But we had won. We had payd our soldatos. We had taken the enemy’s stores and captured a man of the Hegemon’s own blood. For the fyrst time, our company possessed enough coyn to buy weapons, provisiouns, and the serwyces of men who knew how to use both. For the fyrst time, the people who had sheltered us could look at the Hegemon’s power and know that it had been resisted in the open.

The tale would travel. I could not prevent it.

By nyghtfall, it had already begun to grow.

We held Ser Niccolò in a house beyond the villauge, where the windows were narrow and the doors thick. I gave him a clean bed, a physician, and a guaurd who was instructed to treat him with the same courtesy he would offer a merchaunt’s guest.

This did not pleause him.

“I am a prisoner,” he said, when I visited him the following morning.

“Thou art.”

“Then why am I not in chayns?”

“Because chayns cost money, and thou hast not yet proved worth the expense.”

He stared at me.

I drew a chair beside the bed and placed a cup of watered wyne upon the table. “I would speak with thee about thy ransom.”

“I shall pay nothing.”

“That is a matter for thy familie.”

“Herod will not pay a coyn.”

“Perhaps. But thou art his cousin.”

“A distant cousin.”

“Yet close enough to commaund his men and carrie his banner.”

He looked away.

I had studied the familie connectiouns of the Malvezzi before the battle, though I confess I had not expected to capture one of them. Ser Niccolò was the son of a younger branch, related to Herod through a marriage and a grandfather who had died before either of them was born. He was not an heir to the Hegemon’s positioun, nor did he possess any great estate of his own. But he was close enough to the household to be seen at its feasts, and his captivité would be a publick humiliatioun.

The Hegemon could dismiss him as unimportant. He could also ransom him, exchange him, or demaund his release. Each choice would reveal something.

I intended to discover which.

“Tell me,” I said, “what was the convoy carrieing besides grain and iron?”

“Nothing.”

“Then thou wilt not object if I ask the factour.”

He did not answer.

“The chests contained money,” I continued. “Not all the money entered in the accounts, I think. There are sums missing from the factour’s tallie. Perhaps thou knowest where they went.”

“I know nothing of accounts.”

“Then we are both fortunate. I have a clerk who knows a great deal.”

I rose to leave.

“Ferrabosco.”

I tourned.

“You think this victorie makes thee powerful.”

“No. I think it makes me less poore.”

“Herod will come for me.”

“I expect he will.”

“And when he does, he will kill everie man who has aided thee.”

“Perhaps.”

“You speak as if thou dost not care.”

I looked at him. “I care verie much. That is why I have not yet decided what to do with thee.”

He had expected anger, I think, or a threat. He had expected me to declare that I would trade his life for justice, or use him to avenge everie injurie done by his familie. Such declaratiouns are easy to make when one does not have to fulfil them.

I had no intentioun of making one.

“I shall not torture thee,” I said. “I shall not sell thee. I shall not kill thee merelie to demonstrate that I can. But thou shalt remain here until thy familie makes an offer, and thou shalt be treated according to the terms we have agreed.”

“What terms?”

“The terms of a prisoner who is valuable enough to ransom and sensible enough to remain alive.”

He looked at the cup of wyne.

“And if Herod refuses?”

“Then we shall have to find another arrangement.”

I left him with the guaurd.

Outside, Bernat was waiting beside the gate. He had heaurd enough of the conversatioun to understand its purpose, and he looked at me with a mixture of amusement and impatience.

“Thou art holding a Malvezzi,” he said. “A great prize.”

“A man.”

“A man with a familie.”

“A familie which may or may not pay.”

“Then take the money from their londs.”

“That is what I intend to do.”

He laughed. “Thou art a straunge captain. Thou wynest a battle, takest a nobleman, and then speakest of accounts.”

“Accounts are what brought us here.”

“No. Herod brought us here.”

“Herod brought me here. I brought thee here.”

Bernat considered this, then grinned. “That is true. And I shall remember it when I send thee my next bill.”

The news of Niccolò’s capture travelled more quicklie than the news of the battle itself. The lesser Houses began to wonder whether the Hegemon’s protectioun was as certain as they had believed. Merchaunts who had hesitated to lend us money now sent discreet inquiries. Two men who had served in Herod’s retinue offered to provide informatioun in exchange for safe passauge out of Bologne. A noblewoman sent a purse with no letter attached, and I did not ask who had given it.

The Guelphs and Ghibellines began to take an ynterest.

Their ynterest was not in me, of course. It was in the possibilité that a new force myght weaken the Hegemon, and in the questioun of who myght profit if it did. The factiouns had long contended over the balaunce of power in the cities of Emilia. They could be allies at supper and enemies before dawn, and each was accustomed to calling its own ambitioun the cause of peace.

I received a letter from a Guelph agent offering money, arms, and the promise of friends in Florence. It was written in a courteous hond and contained no mentioun of the conditiouns attached. A Ghibelline intermediarie arrived two days later, offering a safe route through the countrieside and the possibilité of an audience with a lorde who disliked Herod’s ascendancy.

I thanked both and promised nothing.

Aldo thought me foolish.

“Take the money,” he said. “We need it.”

“Then we shall owe them.”

“We owe everieone.”

“Not everieone can claim to have purchased us.”

He leaned agaynst the table. “Thou canst not fight a war without allies.”

“Nor canst thou win one if everie allie believes he owns thee.”

He frowned, for he knew I was ryght and disliked it all the more.

The factiouns were not to be dismissed. Their influence could bring us soldatos, money, shelter, and legitimacy. It could also tourn our quarrel into a contest in which the people we meant to defend were merelie pieces upon a boaurd. If I accepted one factioun’s help, the other myght support Herod out of spite. If I accepted both, each would suspect me of betrayal. If I accepted neither, I myght be starved of the means to continue.

There was no clean path through it.

I told the agents that I would receive their messages, but I would swear allegiaunce to neither factioun. I would consider any assistaunce offered without conditiouns that required me to surrender my company’s independence. They departed with polite smiles, which I trusted less than open insults.

Meanwhile, we began to sell the grain and iron.

I did not sell it all at once. A sudden quantité of cheap grain would ruin the pryce and make enemies of everie merchaunt who held a store. We distributed part to the villauges from which the convoy had collected its levies, sold part through intermediaries, and retained enough to feed our own company. The iron went to smiths who agreed to provide us with weapons at a fair rate. Some of the horses were sold; others were kept for the company.

We did not give everiething away. I was not so foolish as to believe that generosité could sustain an army. But we did not keep everiething either. A villauge that has fed us through wynter should not be expected to wautch its childeren go hungrie while we sell grain for profit. Nor did I think it wise to make the people who sheltered us regret their kindnesse.

Our victorie made us richer, but it also made us responsible for more lives.

I was beginning to understand that the two were much the same thing.

Herod’s answer came not by letter, but through a woman who arrived at our camp after midnyght.

She was a servaunt from Bologne, wrapped in a cloak too thin for the cold. Her shoes were torn, and she had walked most of the way from the cité. She asked for me by name and would not speak to anyone else.

I found her beside the fire, shaking so violentlie that she could scarcelie hold the cup Margherita gave her.

“My lorde,” she said, “they are taking the families.”

I sat down opposite her.

“Whose families?”

“The men who serve thee. Those who have left Bologne, those who send thee money, those who carrie thy letters. They have lists. The wautch has gone to the houses. They say the Hegemon has ordered them taken for questiouning.”

“How many?”

She shook her head. “I do not know. Many.”

“Are they being held at the palays?”

“Some. Others at the houses of the Hegemon’s friends. They have taken childeren.”

For a moment, I heaurd nothing but the fire.

I had expected Herod to send soldatos agaynst us. I had expected arrests, confiscatiouns, and the destructioun of any house suspected of giving us shelter. I had even expected him to take hostages from among the families of my captains, though I had hoped that he would not do so before we had become a greater threat.

I had not expected him to move so quicklie.

“Why now?” I asked.

“Because of the Malvezzi,” she said. “Because thou hast taken his cousin. Because the letter hath been read everiewhere. Because the Hegemon says thou meanest to bring the whole countrie agaynst him.”

I thanked her, gave her food, and ordered that she be taken to a safe room. Then I sent for Aldo, Pietro, Adelaide, and the men who knew Bologne best.

We met before dawn.

The lists were incomplete, but the pattern was plain. Herod’s men had taken the wyves and childeren of those who had served in my company, and of several men who had supplied us with food or informatioun. They had also seized the household of a former Malvezzi retainer who had defected to us, and the familie of a clerk who had copied the accounts of the One Way.

The Hegemon had not merelie struck at our company. He had struck at the network that made our company possible.

Aldo was furious.

“We must go back,” he said. “We must take the palays gate, break the prison, and bring them out.”

“With what?” I asked. “We have twentie men fit to fight, and half the Catalans have already departed.”

“Then we recruit more.”

“From where? The villauges Herod has closed? The roads his men are wautching? Shall we gather a hundred men and march upon Bologne, where he has a thousand?”

“We cannot leave them.”

“No,” I said. “We cannot.”

The words seemed to settle upon the room.

I looked at the faces around the table. Pietro was silent, his honds clasped before him. Adelaide had spread the lists across the boaurds and was marking each name with a small stroke. Margherita stood in the doorway, listening. Emiglio had arrived without his usual jokes. The men who had come to me for wauges, protectioun, or revanche were now confronted with a choice that no contract could make easy.

Herod had understood something I had not. A man myght risk his own life for a cause. He myght even risk his fortune. But the moment he believes his wyfe and childeren are to pay the pryce, the cause becomes something verie different.

“Who is in danger?” I asked.

“Everieone named on the lists,” Adelaide replied. “And those whose names they have not yet found.”

“My wyfe?”

She hesitated.

“I do not know.”

I rose so quicklie that the chair fell behind me.

I had left my wyfe and daughter with friends near Bologne, believing that their household was obscure enough to escape notice. I had chosen the place myself. It lay away from the main road, beyond the reach of the Hegemon’s immediate officers, and belonged to a familie with no known connectioun to my affairs. I had thought myself careful.

I had also thought that the Hegemon would seek to defeat me as a captain, rather than punish me as a husband.

There are many things a man can forgive in himself until another person must suffer for them.

I ordered two riders to prepare at once. One would go to the house where my familie was staying; the other would ride to Florence and secure a lodging under another name. They were to take no company, carrie no sign of our cause, and speak to no one unless necessarie. If my wyfe and daughter were safe, they were to leave that verie morning. If they were not, the riders were to find them and bring them out by whatever road remained open.

I gave them nearlie all the money I had kept for my own use.

Then I tourned to the others.

“I will not order any man to remain with us,” I said. “If thou hast a wyfe, a child, a mother, or a broother in Bologne, go to them. I shall not call thee cowaurd, nor take thy wauges, nor deny thee a place if thou retournest.”

Aldo stared at me. “If they all leave, we shall have no company.”

“If I commaund them to stay, we shall have no honour.”

“This is not a matter of honour.”

“No. It is a matter of what we have become.”

I had no wish to be a lorde who spoke of sacrifice from a safe chair. I had no wish to tell a man that his child must remain in danger because the cause required it, while my own familie sat beyond the reach of Herod’s hond. I knew that there were captains who would have called such demaunds necessarie. I knew, too, that they were often the fyrst to send their own households away.

I could not ask another man to bear a burden I had refused to place upon my own shoulders.

But I could not save them all.

That was the truth I had been avoiding, and it stood before me now with no mercy in its face.

Some of the men departed that morning. A few left without speaking. Others embraced their companiouns and promised to retourn. One man, whose wyfe had been taken the nyght before, mounted his horse and rode towaurds Bologne alone. We ne'er saw him agayn.

Pietro remained. So did Adelaide, Margherita, Emiglio, Aldo, and most of the men who had no familie within the cité. Bernat’s Catalans had already received their wauges and departed according to their contract, though six of them had chosen to remain for another fortnyght in exchange for further pyment.

The company was smaller than it had been the day before.

It was also angrier.

I did not permit that anger to govern us. We would not ride blindlie into Bologne, nor would we burn a villauge in revanche for the deeds of the Hegemon’s men. We would gather informatioun, identify where the prisoners were held, and discover which officers had taken charge of them. We would seek an exchange, a ransom, or a means of bringing them out.

But fyrst, I had to know whether my own familie was safe.

The two riders retourned before sunset.

My wyfe and daughter had left the house before the wautch arrived. A neighbour had seen the men approaching and sent word; my wyfe had gathered what she could carrie, taken our daughter by the hond, and gone out through the gaurden gate. They had travelled on foot for part of the way, then joined a merchaunt’s cart heading south. The rider had found them at an inn beyond the cité’s reach, where they were waiting for the second horse.

They were alive. They were free. They were on their way to Florence.

I sat alone after hearing the news.

I ought to have felt relief, and I did. I ought to have thanked God, and I did that too, though I have ne'er been certain that Heaven attends to the prayers of merchaunts. But beneath the relief lay a shame I could not easilie name. My wyfe and daughter were safe because I had had warning, because I had money to send riders, because a neighbour had been brave enough to speak, and because the road south remained open.

Others had none of these advauntages.
