Solar Defence Delivers 450 Nagastra-1R Loitering Munitions to Indian Army in Largest Single Batch
--------------------------------
Solar Defence and Aerospace Limited (SDAL) has completed the delivery of 450 Nagastra-1R loitering munitions to the Indian Army in a single supply batch, marking the largest such handover of these systems so far. The order was placed under emergency procurement after rigorous technical trials. Four companies participated, but only Solar Defence met all operational requirements for accuracy, reliability, and performance.

The Nagastra-1R is an indigenous Indian loitering munition, also known as a kamikaze drone, designed for short-range precision strikes. It features high target hit accuracy, a 360-degree gimbal camera with thermal night vision, and the ability to abort a mission and recover safely if needed. Live-fire trials confirmed its effectiveness across different terrains, including high-altitude areas, with over 80 percent indigenous content and no compromise on quality.

This delivery strengthens the Indian Army’s short-range precision strike capability with a cost-effective, homegrown solution. Amid ongoing regional conflicts, the Nagastra-1R offers a ready indigenous alternative for modern battlefield needs. The system supports faster induction of advanced weapons while reducing dependence on foreign suppliers and boosting India’s defence manufacturing ecosystem under Atmanirbhar Bharat.

📖 DAILY SCRIPTURE
BIRTHING OF A NATION
Faith • Family • Freedom
WEDNESDAY, OCTOBER 14, 2026
WHEN JESUS STOPPED FOR ONE
Mark 10:49 (NLT)
“When Jesus heard him, he stopped and said, ‘Tell him to come here.’”
Imagine sitting beside a busy road, hearing hundreds of footsteps passing by, but never being able to see the faces of those walking past.
Day after day, people come and go. Some drop a coin. Others walk by without acknowledging you.
This was the life of Bartimaeus, a blind beggar sitting beside the road near Jericho.
But one day, something extraordinary happened.
He heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by!
Bartimaeus began shouting, calling upon Jesus to have mercy on him.
The crowd wasn't impressed.
They told him to be quiet!
Imagine that. A man desperately needing help was being silenced by the very people walking alongside Jesus.
But Bartimaeus refused to stop crying out.
And then Scripture records something beautiful.
JESUS STOPPED.
Think about that for a moment.
The Son of God was travelling toward Jerusalem. Crowds surrounded Him. His earthly ministry was moving toward the cross.
Yet in the middle of everything, Jesus heard the cry of one blind man.
He didn't consider Bartimaeus an interruption.
He didn't tell him to wait until He had more time.
He stopped and called him.
And when Bartimaeus came, Jesus asked what he wanted Him to do.
The blind man asked to see.
Jesus responded to his faith, and Bartimaeus received his sight and followed Him down the road.
What a powerful picture of our Saviour!
We live in a world that measures importance by position, popularity, wealth, and influence.
People can feel invisible, forgotten, or unworthy of anyone's attention.
Perhaps you've felt that way yourself.
You pray, but wonder whether heaven hears you.
You look at everything happening around the world and wonder whether your little life really matters.
But remember Bartimaeus.
The crowd heard a disturbance. Jesus heard a soul crying for mercy.
And there's another lesson here.
Sometimes we're so busy with our own schedules, responsibilities, and ambitions that we walk right past the very people God wants us to notice.
Jesus showed us that compassion isn't merely something we talk about.
Sometimes compassion means stopping.
Listening.
Looking someone in the eyes.
And making them feel that their life matters.
The greatest example of God's love is that Jesus Christ came to seek and save the lost. He went to the cross for sinners and rose again, opening the way to forgiveness and eternal life.
If Jesus was willing to stop for Bartimaeus, shouldn't we be willing to stop for someone who needs us today?
And if you're the one crying out for mercy, don't let the voices around you convince you to remain silent.
Keep calling on Jesus.
YOU MAY FEEL INVISIBLE TO THE WORLD, BUT YOU ARE NOT INVISIBLE TO GOD.
🎯 TODAY'S MISSION
Slow down long enough to notice someone you might ordinarily pass by. Listen to them, encourage them, offer practical help, or pray with them. Let someone experience the compassion of Jesus through you.
🙏 PRAYER
Lord Jesus, thank You for hearing the cries of those the world overlooks. Forgive me for the times I've been too busy to notice someone hurting. Give me Your compassion, Your patience, and Your love. Help me hear those who are crying out for mercy, and remind every lonely and discouraged heart that they matter to You. In Jesus' mighty name, Amen.
#FaithFamilyFreedom #DailyScripture #JesusChrist #Bartimaeus #Compassion #Faith #ChristianEncouragement #BirthingOfANation

The Saudi Crown Prince for the thousandth time says No to the PM.... What exactly does the Bibi want from Saudi Arabia?
Yesterday, the Haaretz published a report... It reported that Netanyahu is trying to obtain Saudi approval to join the war against the Houthis..But Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman refused. Yedioth Ahronoth revealed that the Americans discussed with Israeli Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir the possibility of launching Israeli strikes on the Houthis in Yemen... But Zamir refused that and warned that these strikes could lead to escalation with the Houthis and perhaps Iran... In fact, they could cause a delay in the Israeli elections scheduled for October 27!
The Americans want to avoid direct involvement in the war, and the Israeli army warns of escalation that could affect the elections. At the same time, the PM is trying to get Saudi approval to enter the battle! 
If you wanted to enter it, why only through KSA?
Okay... And away from this, why does Netanyahu need Saudi approval in the first place?!
Israel previously bombed the Houthis without Saudi approval it seems that what Netanyahu wants this time bigger than just bombing Houthi sites in Yemen.
4 points
1.Netanyahu wants to enter the Saudi war through the gates of Riyadh itself... So if Saudi Arabia agrees, Israeli intervention will no longer be just an Israeli military operation... But it can be marketed as cooperation with the largest Arab country in confronting a common threat.
For the PM, is a huge political gain. He can try to turn the Saudi-Yemeni war into a gateway to an Arab-Israeli security partnership... And grant Israel a role in a battle that Saudi Arabia did not want to share with it.
2. Elections!
Notice that the Israeli Chief of Staff warned of the possibility of delaying the elections if the confrontation expands.. Can Netanyahu exploit any military participation in Yemen to present himself to the Israeli voter as the man who builds new alliances with the Arabs?
Or can a broad regional war turn into an exceptional circumstance that he can then delaythe elections?!

The project, which KSA obstructed and which aims to connect India to the Arabian Gulf and Europe through a network of ports & railways passing through Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and Israel... Means that Netanyahu may try to open security and political channels with Riyadh... Then use this rapprochement to revive the normalization file... The war on the Houthis becomes, for Israel, an opportunity to achieve goals it could not achieve through diplomacy

This is what can be called "convergence in political outcomes"... Notice that the Houthi escalation creates an opportunity for Bibi to exploit politically... The ability to market the idea of security cooperation with the Kingdom as a shared necessity.
 participation remains before it.. Every Houthi rocket is in Israel's favor, and every Israeli call to Saudi Arabia is is the swap for the Houthis.. A role swap, nothing more, but KSA says no. 
Yhis"no" is not just a refusal of Israeli planes that want to bomb the Houthis... But it may be a refusal to turn the Yemeni war into a bridge that Netanyahu crosses to Riyadh... Then to normalization... Then to regional arrangements he wants to be a central part of... No Bibi, No Trump

الأمريكيون يريدون تجنب التورط المباشر في الحرب والجيش الإسرائيلي يحذر من تصعيد قد يؤثر على الانتخابات...وفي الوقت نفسه نتنياهو يحاول الحصول على موافقة سعودية لدخول المعركة! 
كنت ادخلها يا نتنياهو بالطلب الامريكي لماذا الا عن طريق السعودية!!

وهنا بالنسبة لي تبدأ القصة الحقيقية...

الأولى...نتنياهو يريد الدخول في الحرب السعودية على الحوثي من بوابة الرياض نفسها...فإذا وافقت السعودية، لن يعود التدخل الإسرائيلي مجرد عملية عسكرية إسرائيلية منفردة...بل يمكن تسويقه على أنه تعاون مع أكبر دولة عربية واسلامية في مواجهة خطر مشترك.

وهنا تصبح الحرب على الحوثي بالنسبة لإسرائيل فرصة لتحقيق أهداف لم تستطع تحقيقها عبر الدبلوماسية وحدها.

It was good.

He neither denied nor contradicted essential Christian truths, nor did he make YEC (or Old Earth or Evo or Framework) a condition of faith. Both points matter.

He presented his case gently and patiently, with a substantial background explanation suited to an audience that might disagree with him. I noticed he mentioned RZIM in his opening comments. Ravi Zacharias was a darling of Christian apologists for many years.

I've heard similar reasoning before too. It might be a help Christians whose faith has become overburdened by political and social disputes. I'd share it with dedicated Kent Hovind fans.

The buildup was too long for me. I wanted him to get to the substance sooner, but what I heard remained within the bounds of Christian orthodoxy. :)

The gospel remained intact. He offered ways to address the New Testament's treatment of Adam as an historical person without forcing an either-or conclusion. He left many interpretive questions open.

Finally, he addressed an issue close to my heart:

Making six literal creation days a condition of Christian fellowship is a mistake. 

We should respond, assess, encourage, or admonish Christians working in evolutionary biology, geology, or astronomy by their actual beliefs about Scripture and their faith in the Gospel. 

Their field of study alone does not establish what they believe. Sometimes I wonder how people listen to any of us. Lennox taught with patience.

Alliance for Vietnam's Democracy to Participate in the 2026 Athens Democracy Forum
[Athens, Greece] — [September 27, 2026] — The Alliance for Vietnam's Democracy is proud to announce its participation in the 2026 Athens Democracy Forum, taking place in person from September 29 to October 1 in Athens, Greece. Organized by the Athens Democracy Foundation in association with The New York Times, the Forum convenes global leaders, policymakers, activists, and journalists to address the world's most pressing democratic challenges.
Under the 2026 theme, "Building Order Out of Chaos," the Forum will tackle both the philosophical and operational questions of how democracy must evolve to remain fit for the 21st century. As rising autocrats become emboldened worldwide, the Alliance for Vietnam's Democracy is attending to ensure that the struggle for fundamental human rights and democratic changes in Vietnam remains at the forefront of the global conversation.
"Gathering in Athens, the very cradle of democracy, serves as a powerful reminder that the desire for self-governance is an enduring, universal human right," said Dr. Elise Pham, a member of the Alliance for Vietnam's Democracy’s Steering Committee. "More than two millennia ago, this city proved that governance by the people is possible. Today, as authoritarian regimes contest these ancient ideals globally, the Athens Democracy Forum offers a vital platform to share the Vietnamese people's ongoing fight for liberty and to collaborate with international allies dedicated to democratic renewal."
During the three-day event, representatives from the Alliance will engage with thought leaders, international journalists, and civil society advocates. The 2026 agenda includes rigorous discussions on rethinking governance and security, navigating the digital age, and examining real-time case studies of autocracy and democratic resistance.
By engaging with a diverse network of pro-democracy advocates—including Nobel laureates, reformists, and youth leaders—the Alliance aims to forge new partnerships, elevate awareness of Vietnam's human rights climate, and explore actionable strategies to champion democratic systems that deliver justice, equity and long-term security.
For more information about the 2026 Athens Democracy Forum, visit https://t.co/TQDguZ7o1t.
About the Alliance for Vietnam's Democracy:
The Alliance for Vietnam's Democracy is a coalition of civil societies and political parties dedicated to advocating for human rights and the establishment of a free and democratic Vietnam through non-violent civic engagement and international advocacy.

text:
DEMOCRACY IS BIGGER THAN PARTISAN POLITICS: A RESPONSE TO SHANE CROUCHER’S CRITIQUE OF MARCO RUBIO
Shane Croucher’s “Dissected” commentary in Newsweek offers a satirical interpretation of Marco Rubio’s speech on Western civilization, delivered against the historic backdrop of the Acropolis in Athens. Croucher portrays Rubio’s address as more than a tribute to the intellectual and political inheritance of the West; he interprets it as a calculated political performance, a potential prelude to a presidential campaign, and an attempt to position Rubio as a future leader of the Western world.
Political satire has its place in a free society. Public officials should be scrutinized and their motives questioned. Croucher’s satire repeatedly interprets Rubio’s historical references through the lens of personal ambition, political hypocrisy, and the Trump administration’s conduct.
However, there is a danger when every attempt to expose hypocrisy simultaneously discredits constitutional democracy itself. The democratic tradition of the West is not merely a collection of symbols, architectural styles, imperial ambitions, or rhetorical devices used by politicians seeking power. It is an evolving inheritance of ideas about citizenship, individual liberty, public responsibility, constitutional authority, and the limits of government.
The Acropolis is not simply a picturesque backdrop for a politician’s ambitions. Ancient Greece contributed enduring concepts to political thought, including democracy, civic participation, public debate, and the examination of political authority. It reminds us that democratic ideals must continually be tested against political reality. The strength of the American experiment lies not in a claim of historical perfection, but in the possibility of correcting injustice through institutions, law, civic participation, and peaceful political change.
What distinguishes a constitutional democracy is not the personal virtue of its leaders or the eloquence of their speeches. It is the structure of government and the principles that constrain the exercise of political power. These principles include:
•Government by consent of the governed: Political authority derives from the people through free, fair, and meaningful elections.
•The rule of law: Public officials and ordinary citizens alike are subject to the law, and government cannot legitimately substitute personal preference for constitutional authority.
•An independent judiciary: Courts must be able to interpret and apply the law without improper political interference.
•Checks and balances: Legislative, executive, and judicial institutions exercise distinct constitutional responsibilities, providing safeguards against the concentration and abuse of power.
•Civil liberties and human rights: Freedom of expression, religion, peaceful assembly, association, and due process must be protected.
•Independent journalism and civil society: Citizens need access to information, investigative reporting, and organizations capable of scrutinizing government conduct.
•Political pluralism: Competing parties, opposing viewpoints, and peaceful political movements must have the opportunity to participate in public life.
•Accountability and peaceful transfers of power: Elections, courts, legislative oversight, and other lawful mechanisms must allow citizens to challenge government decisions and replace their representatives.
These are not merely abstract principles; they are the people's safeguards against the abuse of power.
The genius of constitutional government is that it does not require citizens to trust every leader. Instead, it recognizes that leaders are human, that ambition can become excessive, and that even well-intentioned officials can make serious mistakes. Government must therefore be designed to function through established rules and institutional restraints rather than personal loyalty or unquestioning faith in whoever occupies the highest office.
In that sense, checks and balances are among the people's most important political safeguards. They provide lawful means of resisting overreach without resorting to violence, authoritarianism, or the destruction of the political system itself. The executive branch cannot simply claim unlimited authority because it has won an election. The legislature has constitutional responsibilities of its own, and the judiciary must be able to adjudicate legal disputes independently. Elections establish political mandates, but those mandates operate within constitutional limits.
The system is not perfect. Institutional conflict can be frustrating, and constitutional safeguards can sometimes slow government action. But the purpose of those restraints is precisely to prevent speed, popularity, or concentrated authority from becoming substitutes for lawful government. A constitutional democracy is not a system in which one side always wins. It is a system in which no political side is entitled to win everything; by practice and definition, a single-party state is not a democracy.
Accountability requires examining what public officials actually do, not merely assuming that the truth lies halfway between competing accusations. But the same democratic standard must apply regardless of political affiliation. If we defend constitutional restraints when our opponents hold power, we must defend them when our allies do. If we insist on the independence of courts when their decisions favor our side, we must recognize that independence when their decisions disappoint us. If we demand honest journalism about one administration, we must accept scrutiny of another.
Democracy becomes fragile when constitutional principles are treated as partisan weapons rather than common rules. The remedy for the misuse of democratic ideals is not to abandon those ideals. It is to insist that public officials live up to them.
It also means recognizing that democratic values are sought across many civilizations—of the people, by the people, and for the people. People throughout the world have struggled for accountable government, human dignity, freedom, and political participation. Defending Western democracy need not require denying the contributions or aspirations of other civilizations. The enduring value of the Western constitutional tradition is not that it provides a justification for cultural superiority. It is that it offers principles by which political authority can be challenged, limited, and held accountable.
This same responsibility extends to journalists and commentators. A free press must be able to ridicule politicians, expose inconsistencies, challenge official narratives, and question the motives behind public speeches. But the most valuable political commentary does more than assign motives or sharpen partisan divisions. It helps readers distinguish between the failures of individual leaders and the principles that should govern them.
Satire can expose hypocrisy, puncture vanity, and challenge political mythology. But when political commentary becomes so consumed by partisan interpretation that it obscures the constitutional principles at stake, it risks contributing to the very cynicism that weakens democratic life.
The answer is not to demand that journalists praise Western civilization or spare conservative politicians from criticism. It is to insist on a more rigorous standard: criticize leaders with evidence, assess policies against constitutional principles, acknowledge failures wherever they occur, and preserve the distinction between a political faction and the democratic system that allows factions to compete peacefully.
The people's power does not rest in finding a flawless leader. It rests in maintaining a system in which no leader is beyond scrutiny, no administration is above the law, and no political faction can legitimately claim permanent ownership of the state. That is the democratic inheritance worth defending.
The Acropolis may remind us of the origins of political ideas that continue to shape our world, but the American Constitution reminds us of something equally important: those ideas survive only when citizens and institutions put them into practice. Democracy is not the unquestioning celebration of Western civilization, nor is it the reflexive rejection of anyone who invokes it. Democracy is the continuing effort to make government accountable to the people, to restrain power through law, and to preserve the freedom to disagree without destroying the institutions that make disagreement possible.

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

$PROF: TULSA-PRO is getting attention beyond the hospital walls.

Congressman Gus Bilirakis and Congresswoman Laurel Lee recently visited BayCare Hospital Wesley Chapel to learn firsthand about the TULSA Procedure.

That’s an encouraging development for Profound Medical ($PROF / $PRN.TO).

Why does it matter?

TULSA-PRO uses real-time MRI guidance and targeted ultrasound to treat prostate tissue without an incision. Its potential value extends beyond technology: it offers another treatment option for men facing prostate cancer and other prostate conditions.

When elected representatives engage directly with a technology at a treating hospital, it creates an opportunity to raise awareness of men’s health, innovation and access to advanced care.

But let’s keep the distinction clear: this visit is not an endorsement, government funding announcement or reimbursement decision. The commercial impact remains to be demonstrated.

For my investment thesis, the bigger picture is what matters: clinical evidence, hospital adoption, patient awareness and treatment access all need to develop together.

Profound’s challenge now is to turn growing awareness into measurable outcomes—more installations, more procedures per system and stronger recurring revenue.

A promising technology becomes a valuable business when adoption translates into sustained utilization.

I’m watching that conversion closely.

text:
He argued both parties had “sold us out,” but singled out the Democrats as “more racist.” His primary evidence was the composition of national power: key government positions were held by Democrats from Southern states he called “cracker states” (Georgia, Alabama, Texas, Mississippi, etc.). He pointed to the President (Lyndon B. Johnson of Texas) and argued that Southern Democrats, through seniority, controlled major congressional committees and therefore the levers of federal power. In his view, Democratic control of the White House and Congress did not produce meaningful gains for Black people; instead, it entrenched the power of segregationists who blocked or diluted civil rights measures. He rejected the idea that a Southern Democrat ceased being a racist upon gaining higher office, stating that “just because a cracker becomes president he ceases being a cracker.”
This fit a consistent theme in his 1964 speeches. He described Dixiecrats as Democrats “in disguise,” noted that Black voters had given decisive support to Democrats who then failed to deliver, and warned that party loyalty kept Black political power subordinated Malcolm X’s critique of Democratic racism, especially in his June 28, 1964 Organization of Afro-American Unity (OAAU) founding speech, centered on the claim that the Democratic Party was not merely inadequate but structurally more harmful to Black Americans than the Republican Party at that time.
He also distinguished between open Southern Democrat conservatives (“wolves”) and Northern white Democrat liberals (“foxes”), arguing the latter were often more dangerous because they offered rhetorical support while preserving the underlying power structure.
He used the fox/wolf metaphor repeatedly in 1963–1964. The wolf was the open Southern segregationist (often a Dixiecrat). The fox was the Northern white liberal who smiled, spoke of friendship and integration, and sought Black political support while, in his view, preserving the same underlying power structure. At the time, Northern white liberals were overwhelmingly Democrats, and the Democratic Party as a whole contained both the Northern liberal wing and the Southern segregationist wing that controlled key congressional power through seniority.

text:
Nine Harlem mothers built their children a school in a church basement in 1958, then shut it down on purpose. They had volunteers teaching English, math, French, and art appreciation, and it was working, and that was the problem.

As long as those children were learning something, the Board of Education had no reason to prosecute anybody, and without a prosecution no judge would ever be made to look inside the real schools. So they took the classes away from their own kids and sat down to wait for the city.

Thirty-one days after four girls were killed in the basement of a church in Birmingham, a man walked into a room full of New York City schoolteachers and told them they were living through a very dangerous time. He did not have to explain which dangerous time he meant.

It was October 16, 1963, and everybody sitting in front of him had read the same newspapers he had. Addie Mae Collins was fourteen, Carole Robertson was fourteen, Cynthia Wesley was fourteen, and Denise McNair was eleven.

James Baldwin told that room the country was not being menaced by Khrushchev. It was being menaced from the inside, by itself, and the teachers in those chairs were part of the machinery doing it.

Then he did something you would not expect from the most famous Black writer in America.

He apologized for being there.

He told them he was not a teacher himself, that he was fairly easily intimidated, and asked them to bear with him. The man who had been on the cover of Time magazine five months earlier, whose book had come out in January and moved through the country like weather, stood in front of a room of public school employees and admitted he was nervous.

Then he stopped being nervous.

He walked them through what education actually is, from the beginning, like he was explaining it to children. A child gets born, somebody takes on the duty of civilizing that child, and the civilizing happens inside a society that has its own reasons for wanting the job done a particular way.

His example was not Alabama. His example was Germany.

Children raised and schooled to the purposes of the Third Reich, he said, came out barbarians. He was standing in New York City telling American teachers, to their faces, that a school system can manufacture cruelty and hand out diplomas for it.

Then came the sentence.

The paradox of education is precisely this, he told them, and then he finished the thought. The moment a person begins to wake up is the same moment that person begins to examine the society that is doing the teaching.

That is the line you have seen a thousand times, on mugs and T-shirts and classroom walls, on a black square with white letters going around your feed on a Tuesday afternoon. He was not offering it as inspiration.

He was handing out an assignment, and he knew what it would cost the people he handed it to. Because the next thing out of his mouth was about Birmingham.

He told them there must have been a day in this country when children being bombed in Sunday school would have caused a public uproar and put a governor's career in real danger. It happened, he said, and there was no uproar.

Here is the part that falls off the poster.

Baldwin was not in that room to talk about Alabama. He was talking about the school system those teachers worked for.

To make it plain he built them a scene, and it is worth walking through slowly, because it is the whole speech in miniature. Picture a Black boy, seven years old, and a father who decides to take him downtown for the afternoon.

They get on a bus at 131st Street and Seventh Avenue and ride down through the park. They come out the other side into a city that is a few miles and one entire world away from the place they got on.

The Park Avenue the boy lives near is dark and dirty, and nobody is opening a Tiffany's on it. The Park Avenue at the far end of the ride has doormen, and the garbage gets collected, and people walk around like they own the ground under their feet, because they do.

Nobody has to explain any of this to the child.

He works it out himself, and Baldwin told them it gets into a child's head much earlier than adults are comfortable admitting.

A few years on the same boy is a grocery boy or a messenger, and he tries a front entrance, and a man tells him to go around to the back door. Later still, if he happens to know somebody in that building, the same man wants to know where his package is.

Baldwin knew that bus route because he had ridden it. He told the room he had come up a street boy himself, so none of this was theory to him.

Then he turned it around on them and told them what he would do with a Black child if the child were his to teach. He said he would tell that child straight out that the streets and the buildings and the dangers pressing in on him were criminal, and that none of it was an accident.

He said he would make him understand that the real history of this country is bigger and uglier and more beautiful than anything he had ever been handed in a classroom, that the world is bigger still, and that all of it belongs to him.

Near the end he said the poster sentence over again, in harder words.

At the exact moment you develop a conscience, he told them, you are going to find yourself at war with your own country. And if you think of yourself as an educated person, changing that country is your job.

Now here is why that man had the standing to say it in that room.

He was not describing a school system from the outside. He was describing the one that made him, and he could name the people in it.

At P.S. 24 in Harlem the principal was Gertrude Ayer, the first Black woman to run a public school in New York City, and she looked at a small odd boy with enormous eyes and decided he was worth extra trouble. She put him with a young white teacher from the Midwest named Orilla Miller, who he called Bill.

Miller took him to his first play, argued books with him, and quietly funneled help to a family that had close to nothing.

Then he went on to Frederick Douglass Junior High School, at 120 West 140th Street.

Inside that building a Harvard-trained math teacher named Herman Porter walked him into the 42nd Street library for the first time in his life. And inside that building Countee Cullen, the Harlem Renaissance poet, taught him French and put him to work on the school paper.

Cullen is the one who told him to apply to DeWitt Clinton, which is where he met Richard Avedon and started editing magazines. Four people, all of them New York City public school employees, built James Baldwin out of a poor kid from 131st Street.

So when he told that room in 1963 that a teacher's real job is to put a weapon in a child's hand, he was not speculating. Now hold on to that address, because this is where the story you have never been told begins.

Frederick Douglass Junior High School had a number.

It was Junior High School 139.

In December 1957 a teacher in that building named Harcourt Tynes gave his ninth grade class an assignment. Go up to the Schomburg, he told them, and write a book of biographies of Black people.

His students wrote it and illustrated it by hand, with help from the school librarian and the art teacher, and bound it into a volume that sits in the New York Public Library today. That is exactly what Baldwin would stand up and demand six years later, and it was already happening inside his old junior high school.

Nine months after those boys finished their book, mothers in Harlem said they would go to jail and rot there before they let their own children walk into Junior High School 139.

There were nine of them, and their children were zoned into three Harlem junior highs. Junior High School 136, Junior High School 139, and Junior High School 120.

They knew those buildings from the inside. Overcrowded, dirtier, thinner curriculum, fewer resources, and more teachers standing in front of classrooms without a license to be there.

Brown v. Board of Education was four years old by then and nobody had ever pointed it at New York. That was the trick of it up North, no sign on the door and no governor blocking the entrance, just zoning maps, and the maps did the work quietly.

The Board of Education called it de facto, the result of housing patterns.

Nobody's fault.

One of those mothers was Mae Mallory, who had come up in Macon, Georgia, and had two children. In January 1957 she went down to a Board of Education hearing and said it out loud to the people who ran the schools.

Her daughter Patricia's school in Harlem, she told them, was just as "Jim Crow" as the Hazel Street School she herself had attended back in Macon. She used the Southern word on purpose, in a New York hearing room, to New Yorkers who were certain the word did not apply to them.

That September the parents went down to City Hall. Ella Baker was there with them, fifteen parents in all, sitting across from Mayor Robert Wagner and his school officials.

They got nothing.

In October 1958 they sued, asking a million dollars in damages and accusing the Board of a sinister and discriminatory purpose in keeping Harlem's schools segregated. The New York Times ran it as Harlem parents filing for a million.

Then the case sat there. Lawsuits are slow and children are not, and a seventh grader does not get that year back while lawyers file paper.

So at the start of the school year the mothers stopped sending their children in. Fifteen parents began it, and they were not willing to let their children go ignorant to make a point, so they built a school.

A Harlem minister named Eugene Callender opened his church for them. Volunteers came in to teach, and the parents' own lawyer and his wife took classes themselves.

Those children were taught English, math, social studies, world events, music, French, and art appreciation.

Art appreciation.

In a borrowed church room in Harlem in 1958, somebody stood in front of Black children and taught them how to look at a painting. And then the mothers shut it down.

Not because it failed. Because it worked, and working was the trap.

New York State law said a child had to be in school, and a parent who kept a child out could be fined or sent to prison. But their children were in school, learning more than they had been learning before.

Which meant the Board had no case to bring, and with no case there was no courtroom. And with no courtroom, no judge in the state of New York would ever be forced to look at what was inside 136, 139, and 120.

Their lawyer, Paul Zuber, understood the arithmetic.

The only way to be heard was to be prosecuted.

So the mothers ended the classes. They walked into that church, stopped the one good thing they had built, and sent their own children home to sit, so that the city would finally have a reason to come after them.

Some of the parents could not do it, and nobody should blame them. That is where fifteen became nine.

Understand what was being asked here.

Not a march, not a sign, not one hard afternoon.

They were being asked to keep their own children out of school on purpose, indefinitely, and to look like bad mothers in public the entire time. The city obliged them exactly.

On October 28, 1958, the Board of Education brought the parents in, in two separate cases. The charge was not truancy.

The charge was neglect.

The word the State of New York put on paper for those women was neglect. On December 4 the Times ran it plain, four mothers guilty in the school boycott, in front of family court judge Nathaniel Kaplan.

Four of them stood in a courtroom and were told they had neglected their children. Eleven days later, two of the others drew a different judge.

Her name was Justine Wise Polier, and the case in front of her carried a caption that ought to be carved into the side of the Board of Education building. In the matter of Charlene Skipwith and Sheldon Rector, children twelve years of age.

Two twelve year olds, entered in the record as neglected.

The parents did not come in with speeches. They came in with documented conditions inside those schools, and the pattern showing the same conditions turning up wherever the students were Black and Puerto Rican, and not turning up where the students were white.

On December 15, 1958, Polier dismissed the charges. She wrote that those children had been getting inferior educational opportunities in those schools by reason of racial discrimination.

If the city handed a child a discriminatory education, she ruled, the city could not then force that child to attend.

It was the first time a Northern court put it in writing.

Here is what it bought them. The Board agreed to transfer the nine mothers' own children into better schools, and for every other child in Harlem the schools stayed exactly as they were.

The million dollar damages suit went nowhere. And Mae Mallory, already watched by the FBI for years, went down to North Carolina afterward to support Freedom Riders, got accused of kidnapping, and spent years in a prison cell in Cleveland before leaving the country for good.

That is the receipt on a mother who wanted her daughter in a decent school.

All of that happened five years before Baldwin walked into that room and told those teachers to examine their own society. He was not asking them to imagine something.

And one hundred and ten days after he said it, the city answered him. Monday, February 3, 1964, roughly 460,000 New York City schoolchildren did not go to class, close to half the entire system.

Reverend Milton Galamison built it after the Board offered him integration spread across five more years and he refused to wait them out. Annie Stein organized alongside him, and Bayard Rustin ran the logistics five months after running the March on Washington.

There were picket lines outside hundreds of schools, and freedom schools opened in churches to teach Black history for the day. Then a march went on foot across the Brooklyn Bridge to the Board of Education on Livingston Street.

Bigger than the March on Washington, and by the numbers it still stands as the largest civil rights demonstration in American history.

You were probably never taught that it happened.

Read what those children were asking for and you are reading Baldwin's October talk back to him. They wanted children who looked like them in the pictures in the reading books, and Black contributions to history put into the textbooks properly.

They wanted Black principals, and a real number of Black teachers instead of a token. They wanted a child to be able to open a schoolbook and find himself inside it.

Baldwin had already put that in the title. The night he gave the talk it was called The Negro Child: His Self-Image, and the version the country kept is called A Talk to Teachers, named for the grown people in the chairs.

Sixty-some years on, New York State is still the most segregated state in the country for Black students.

In 2018 ninety percent of Black students in New York attended schools that were predominantly nonwhite, and the average Black student in the state sits in a building where roughly fifteen out of every hundred classmates are white.

Not Mississippi. New York.

He told them to examine the society that was educating them, and people have been quoting it ever since as though it were a thought. It was not a thought, because the society that educated him had a street address.

One hundred twenty West 140th Street, Junior High School 139, where Countee Cullen taught him French and told him he was going to be somebody. Twenty years after he walked out of that building, mothers in his own neighborhood stood in a family court rather than send their children into it.

One of them was Viola Waddy, and she had no podium, no publisher, and no magazine cover.

What she had was a reporter from the Amsterdam News named Sara Slack, a notebook, and a court date already on the calendar.

She told Slack they would go to jail and rot there if that was what it took, and their children still were not going into 136, 139, or 120. The Amsterdam News printed it on December 13, 1958, using her own words for the headline.

We'd rather go to jail.

Baldwin gave that idea its most beautiful words, and it deserves every screen it travels on. Nine women in Harlem had already paid its price, in a family court, in December, with their children's names typed onto the paperwork.

Charlene Skipwith. Sheldon Rector.

Twelve years old, filed as neglected.

Next time that sentence comes across your screen on a black square, put their names underneath it.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

https://t.co/Vm6JEQzdIW

text:
ANNALS OF THE DAY 🪔

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

A Historical Chronicle: October 14 Edition

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

EPIGRAPH

“We carry yesterday like a lantern—not to live in its light, but to see how far we’ve already come, and how much farther we need to go.” ~ Hodgepodgery

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

INTRO

Today’s chronicle journeys from the decisive clash at Hastings that reshaped medieval British leadership to supersonic breakthroughs high above Earth. We celebrate pioneering minds who challenged boundaries in literature, athletics, and aviation while honoring remarkable figures whose legacies continue to inspire. Across centuries of human endeavor, October 14 highlights moments of extraordinary courage and enduring transformation.

────────────── ◈ ──────────────

CALENDAR OVERVIEW 🧭

October 14 is the 287th day of the year in the Gregorian calendar, representing 78.63% of the year completed. A total of 78 days remain after this date, accounting for 21.37% of the year. The year 2026 is a standard common year, not a leap year. This date falls on a Wednesday during ISO week number 42. Verified observances for today include World Standards Day, recognized globally to honor the efforts of standardization experts, and National Education Day in Poland, commemorating the establishment of the Commission of National Education in 1773.

───────────────────────────────────

🏛️ MAJOR HISTORICAL EVENTS

Moments of political realignment and momentous conflict defined this day throughout world history.

1066 — The Battle of Hastings

King Harold II of England confronted the invading Norman force led by William, Duke of Normandy, near Hastings. The grueling battle ended with the death of Harold II and a decisive Norman victory, bringing Anglo-Saxon royal rule to an end and beginning the Norman Conquest of England.

🧩 TRIVIA: The famous Bayeux Tapestry visually chronicles the events leading up to and during the battle.

🔥 AFTERMATH: William was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day of that same year.

1322 — Battle of Old Byland

Robert the Bruce's Scottish forces defeated an English army at the Battle of Old Byland in Yorkshire, strengthening Scotland's position in the Wars of Scottish Independence. England formally recognized Scotland's independence in the Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton in 1328.

🧩 TRIVIA:  The Scottish victory was remarkable for its daring battlefield maneuver: Highland troops climbed steep cliffs to outflank the English army, attacking from ground the English apparently considered too difficult to scale. King Edward II fled so hastily from nearby Rievaulx Abbey that he abandoned personal possessions.

1586 — Trial of Mary, Queen of Scots

Mary, Queen of Scots, appeared before a commission at Fotheringhay Castle on October 14–15, 1586. She challenged the commission's authority and disputed its right to try her, while the proceedings lacked the protections expected in a modern criminal trial.

🧩 TRIVIA: Mary was denied legal counsel and shown only copies of the letters against her, yet she spoke in her own defense. The central issue was whether her letters showed she had approved the Babington Plot to assassinate Queen Elizabeth I and place Mary on the English throne. The commission’s guilty verdict followed on October 25, and the evidence and interpretation of her role remain historically debated.

1773 — Establishment of Poland’s Commission of National Education

King Stanisław August Poniatowski created the Commission of National Education in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. It is widely recognized as the world's first formal ministry of education.

🧩 TRIVIA: The commission overhauled university curricula and prioritized teaching in the Polish language over Latin.

1806 — The Battles of Jena and Auerstedt

Napoleon Bonaparte's French forces decisively defeated the Prussian military at the twin battles of Jena and Auerstedt. The defeats led to the French occupation of much of Prussia and a major reorganization of Prussian political and military institutions in the years that followed. 

🧩 TRIVIA: Prussian officer Carl von Clausewitz, later the author of On War, fought at Auerstedt and was captured two weeks later at Prenzlau.

1912 — Theodore Roosevelt Survives an Assassination Attempt

While campaigning for president in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, former U.S. President Theodore Roosevelt was shot in the chest by John Schrank. The bullet passed through the folded manuscript of his speech and his eyeglasses case before lodging in his chest. Despite being wounded, Roosevelt continued addressing the crowd before seeking medical treatment.

🧩 TRIVIA: Roosevelt famously opened his address by declaring to the audience that it took more than that to kill a bull moose.

1944 — Erwin Rommel Forced to Commit Suicide

Field Marshal Erwin Rommel, implicated in the July 20 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler, was offered a choice between facing a public trial with severe consequences for his family or taking cyanide. He chose suicide to protect his family and retain his military honors.

🧩 TRIVIA: The German public was initially told Rommel had succumbed to injuries sustained in an Allied airstrike.

1962 — Start of the Cuban Missile Crisis

A U.S. U-2 reconnaissance aircraft piloted by Major Richard Heyser flew over Cuba and photographed Soviet medium-range ballistic missile sites under construction. The photographic evidence prompted President John F. Kennedy to order a naval quarantine of Cuba and led to an intense diplomatic standoff.

🧩 TRIVIA: The high-altitude images were analyzed at the National Photographic Interpretation Center in Washington, D.C.

1964 — Brezhnev Replaces Khrushchev

The Soviet Communist Party’s Central Committee removed Nikita Khrushchev as First Secretary and installed Leonid Brezhnev; Alexei Kosygin became Premier.

🧩 TRIVIA: Ousted in a largely bloodless party coup in October 1964 while on vacation, Khrushchev was succeeded by Brezhnev, who ruled for nearly 18 years and presided over an era of political stagnation.

1964 — Martin Luther King Jr. Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize

The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that civil rights leader Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his nonviolent resistance against racial prejudice in the United States. At age 35, he became the youngest male recipient of the Peace Prize at the time.

🧩 TRIVIA: Dr. King donated the entirety of his prize money to various civil rights organizations. 

───────────────────────────────────

🚀 SCIENTIFIC, TECHNOLOGICAL, AND CULTURAL MILESTONES

Invention, flight, and creative expression marked key turning points on October 14.

1892 — The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes

Arthur Conan Doyle publishes "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes," a collection of 12 stories originally published serially in "The Strand Magazine"

🧩 TRIVIA: Published in 1892, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes helped transform Sherlock Holmes into a literary sensation. The 12 stories first appeared in The Strand Magazine, where Sidney Paget’s now-iconic illustrations helped establish Holmes’s familiar image, including his deerstalker cap—a look so strongly associated with the detective that it overshadowed the fact that Doyle’s original descriptions did not consistently portray him wearing one.

1926 — Publication of Winnie-the-Pooh

British author A. A. Milne (whose full name was Alan Alexander Milne) published his celebrated children’s book Winnie-the-Pooh, illustrated by E. H. Shepard. The book introduced beloved characters such as Piglet, Eeyore, Owl, and Rabbit to readers around the world.

🧩 TRIVIA: Christopher Robin Milne named his teddy bear partly after Winnipeg, a Canadian black bear at the London Zoo; “Pooh” came from a swan.

1947 — Breaking the Sound Barrier

U.S. Air Force Captain Chuck "Mr. Supersonic" Yeager piloted the Bell X-1 rocket-powered aircraft, named Glamorous Glennis, over the Mojave Desert to achieve the first crewed supersonic flight in history. The aircraft reached a speed of Mach 1.06 at an altitude of 43,000 feet.

🧩 TRIVIA: Yeager flew with two broken ribs sustained in a horse-riding accident two days prior.

💡 INNOVATION: The X-1 featured thin, non-swept wings designed specifically to withstand transonic shock waves.

1968 — First Live Television Broadcast from a U.S. Crewed Spacecraft

The crew of Apollo 7, consisting of Walter "Wally" Schirra, Donn "Whatshisname" Eisele, and Walter "Walt" Cunningham, conducted the first live television transmission from a crewed U.S. spacecraft. The regular broadcasts were known colloquially as the "Wally, Walt, and Donn Show."

🧩 TRIVIA: The crew received an Emmy Award following their mission for their educational broadcasts from orbit.  

───────────────────────────────────

🎂 FAMOUS BIRTHDAYS

Warm wishes and recognition for these notable figures born on October 14, whose lives and achievements span generations and fields of endeavor!

1644 — William Penn

English Philosopher, Quaker and founder of Pennsylvania (No cross, no crown), born in London.

🧩 TRIVIA: William Penn (1644–1718), a Quaker, founded Pennsylvania as a haven for religious freedom; King Charles II named the colony in honor of Penn’s father, Admiral Sir William Penn. His 1682 Frame of Government promoted representative government and religious tolerance, making the colony an influential experiment in liberty.

🎭 TWIST: Penn planned Philadelphia as a gridded city of public squares, a layout that became a model for later American cities.

1882 — Éamon de Valera

Irish statesman who served as Taoiseach (1937–48, 1951–54, 1957–59) and President of Ireland (1959–73), born in New York City.

🧩 TRIVIA: Éamon de Valera took part in the 1916 Easter Rising, founded Fianna Fáil in 1926, and helped shape Ireland’s 1937 Constitution and its World War II neutrality policy.

1890 — Dwight D. Eisenhower

34th US President. Republican (1953-61), and WWII army General, born in Denison, Texas.

🧩 TRIVIA: Eisenhower commanded the Allied D-Day invasion (June 6, 1944), later becoming the 34th U.S. president (1953–1961), nicknamed “Ike.” In 1956, he created the Interstate Highway System, inspired partly by a 1919 Army convoy that took 62 days to travel 3,251 miles across America.

1927 — Sir Roger Moore

He was a British actor best known for portraying secret agent James Bond in seven films, from Live and Let Die (1973) to A View to a Kill (1985), as well as Simon Templar in The Saint and Lord Brett Sinclair in The Persuaders!. He was born in Stockwell, London, England.

🧩 TRIVIA: Roger Moore served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador from 1991 and was knighted in 2003.

1939 — Ralph Lauren (age 87)

He is an iconic American fashion designer and business executive known worldwide for founding the Ralph Lauren Corporation and crafting classic American lifestyle designs. Born in the Bronx, New York.

🧩 TRIVIA: He began his career designing wide, colorful neckties and launched his Polo line in 1967.

1940 — Cliff Richard (age 86)

English rock vocalist ("Move It"; "Living Doll"; "We Don't Talk Anymore"), born in Lucknow, British India.

🧩 TRIVIA: “Move It” (1958), widely considered one of Britain’s first authentic rock ’n’ roll hits, was originally intended as the B-side of “Schoolboy Crush” before reaching No. 2 on the UK chart. 

1968 — Matthew Le Tissier (age 58)

He is a former English professional footballer renowned for his technical skill and loyalty to Southampton Football Club. Born in Saint Peter Port, Guernsey.

🧩 TRIVIA: He converted 47 out of 48 penalty kicks during his professional career.

1974 — Natalie Maines (age 52)

She is an American singer and songwriter best known as the lead vocalist for the Grammy Award-winning country music band The Chicks. Born in Lubbock, Texas.

🧩 TRIVIA: She attended the Berklee College of Music on a full scholarship before joining the band.

1978 — Usher (age 48)

He is an acclaimed American singer, songwriter, and dancer who became one of the best-selling musical artists of the 2000s with hits like "Yeah!" and "U Got It Bad." Born in Dallas, Texas.

🧩 TRIVIA: He joined a local youth church choir in Chattanooga, Tennessee, at the age of nine.

1979 — Stacy Keibler (age 47)

She is an American actress, model, and former professional wrestler who rose to prominence in World Championship Wrestling and WWE. Born in Rosedale, Maryland.

🧩 TRIVIA: She began taking dance lessons at the age of three in ballet, tap, and jazz.

1980 — Ben Whishaw (age 46)

He is an award-winning English actor known for his acclaimed roles on stage and screen, including playing Q in the James Bond series and voicing Paddington Bear. Born in Clifton, Bedfordshire, England.

🧩 TRIVIA: He won the 2013 BAFTA TV Award for Best Actor for playing the title role in *Richard II* in *The Hollow Crown*.

1992 — Ahmed Musa (age 34)

He is a prominent Nigerian professional footballer who became the first Nigerian to score more than once in a FIFA World Cup match. Born in Jos, Nigeria.

🧩 TRIVIA: He scored two goals against Argentina in the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil.

1993 — Charlie Kirk

American conservative political activist (co-founder of Turning Point USA), author, and media figure, born in Arlington Heights, Illinois.

🧩 TRIVIA: He co-founded Turning Point USA in 2012, at age 18.

🎉 Happy birthday to them all!

───────────────────────────────────

🥀 MEMORIAM

We honor the lives and enduring contributions of leaders, artists, and pioneers in diplomacy, cinema, and literature.

1066 — Harold II (aged 44)

Last crowned Anglo-Saxon King of England, who won the Battle of Stamford Bridge in September 1066. He was killed at the Battle of Hastings.

🧩 TRIVIA: Harold fought two major battles in 1066 within roughly three weeks. He defeated the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on September 25, then marched south to face William, Duke of Normandy, at the Battle of Hastings on October 14. Harold was killed at Hastings, and William subsequently became king of England.

❓ DID YOU KNOW‽: The famous Bayeux Tapestry depicts a figure with an arrow near his eye and another figure being struck down. The Latin inscription reads “Here King Harold is killed.” However, historians cannot establish with complete certainty whether the arrow-in-the-eye figure is Harold himself.

1941 — Hjalmar Söderberg (aged 72)

A major Swedish author, novelist, and playwright celebrated for his realistic portrayals of turn-of-the-century Stockholm in novels such as *Doctor Glas*. He passed away in Copenhagen, Denmark.

🧩 TRIVIA: His novel *Doctor Glas* remains one of the most widely read and debated classics in Swedish literature.

1944 — Erwin Rommel (aged 52)

German World War II Field Marshal known as the Desert Fox for his command in North Africa and the defense of Normandy. He took his own life under duress after being implicated in the July 20 plot against Adolf Hitler.

🧩 TRIVIA: Rommel became known as the “Desert Fox” for his unpredictable, aggressive tactics in North Africa. His fame was amplified by German propaganda and, interestingly, by the respect he earned from Allied opponents.

1959 — Errol Flynn (aged 50)

An Australian-born American actor famous for his charismatic swashbuckling roles in classic Hollywood films such as *The Adventures of Robin Hood*. He died of a massive heart attack after falling ill in Vancouver, Canada.

🧩 TRIVIA: Before moving to Hollywood, he worked as a gold prospector and tobacco plantation manager in Papua New Guinea.

1977 — Bing Crosby (aged 74)

A legendary American singer and actor whose smooth baritone voice made him one of the best-selling recording artists of the 20th century with hits such as "White Christmas." He collapsed and died of a sudden heart attack while walking off a golf course in Madrid, Spain.

🧩 TRIVIA: His recording of "White Christmas" remains one of the best-selling physical singles of all time worldwide.

1990 — Leonard Bernstein (aged 72)

An influential American conductor, composer, and pianist who composed the musical score for *West Side Story* and served as music director of the New York Philharmonic. He died of a heart attack caused by progressive lung failure at his home in New York City.

🧩 TRIVIA: He conducted a historic performance of Beethoven's Symphony No. 9 in Berlin to celebrate the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.

2010 — Benoit Mandelbrot (aged 85)

A Polish-born French and American mathematician who developed fractal geometry and coined the term "fractal" to describe complex mathematical shapes found in nature. He died of pancreatic cancer in a hospice in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

🧩 TRIVIA: He spent much of his research career working at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center.

2022 — Robbie Coltrane (aged 72)

A beloved Scottish actor and comedian who gained international renown playing Rubeus Hagrid in the *Harry Potter* film series and Dr. Eddie "Fitz" Fitzgerald in *Cracker*. He died of multiple organ failure following a period of declining health in Larbert, Scotland.

🧩 TRIVIA: He took his stage name "Coltrane" in tribute to the famed jazz saxophonist John Coltrane.

───────────────────────────────────

🏟️ SPORTS HIGHLIGHTS

Remarkable athletic victories and historic speed marks highlight October 14 in sports.

1949 — Charles Knocks Out Valentino

Ezzard Charles knocked out Pat Valentino in the eighth round to retain the heavyweight boxing title.

🧩 TRIVIA: Valentino, a 5-to-1 underdog, was ahead on two of the three judges’ scorecards entering the round. The bout at California’s Cow Palace was the first heavyweight championship fight in California since 1909.

1968 — Jim "Oops" Hines Breaks the 10-Second Barrier at the Olympics  At the Summer Olympics in Mexico City, American sprinter Jim Hines won the 100-meter gold medal with an official electronic time of 9.95 seconds. His performance established the first official electronically timed world record under 10 seconds.

1992 — “The Slide” Sends the Braves to the World Series

In Game 7 of the National League Championship Series at Atlanta–Fulton County Stadium, the Braves trailed the Pittsburgh Pirates 2–0 in the bottom of the ninth inning. Francisco Cabrera’s two-out pinch-hit single scored David Justice and Sid Bream, giving Atlanta a 3–2 victory.

🧩 TRIVIA: Bream, slowed by multiple knee surgeries, slid home just ahead of Barry Bonds’ throw.

2003 — The Steve Bartman Incident in Game 6 of the NLCS

During Game 6 of the National League Championship Series between the Chicago Cubs and Florida Marlins, a fan named Steve Bartman attempted to catch a foul ball, deflecting it away from Cubs outfielder Moises "Mo" Alou. The Marlins subsequently scored eight runs in the eighth inning to win the game 8–3 and went on to win the series.

🧩 TRIVIA: In 2017, the Chicago Cubs presented Bartman with an official 2016 World Series championship ring.

2012 — Felix Baumgartner's Record-Breaking Stratospheric Jump

Austrian skydiver Felix "Fearless Felix" Baumgartner jumped from a helium balloon in the stratosphere at an altitude of approximately 127,852 feet (about 39 kilometers) over Roswell, New Mexico. He reached a top speed of 843.6 mph (1,357.6 km/h), becoming the first person to break the sound barrier without vehicle power during freefall.

🧩 TRIVIA: Over 8 million viewers watched the jump live on YouTube, setting a record for live streaming.

───────────────────────────────────

📝 HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY  October 14, 2026

❓ Question: What aircraft did Captain Chuck Yeager pilot on October 14, 1947, when he became the first person to officially break the sound barrier?

[A] The Spirit of St. Louis

[B] The Bell X-1

[C] The Lockheed U-2

[D] The North American X-15 

✅ Answer: [B] The Bell X-1. Captain Chuck Yeager piloted the Bell X-1 rocket-powered aircraft, nicknamed Glamorous Glennis, to Mach 1.06 (about 700 mph) over the Mojave Desert.

───────────────────────────────────

CLOSING

From the battlefield of Hastings to the upper reaches of the stratosphere, October 14 reminds us of humanity's unrelenting urge to push boundaries. Whether through the timeless words of A.A. Milne or the pioneering geometry of Benoit Mandelbrot, the milestones of this date reveal how vision and daring shape our shared story. As we reflect on these achievements, we draw inspiration to confront new horizons with equal measure of courage and resolve.

───────────────────────────────────

LET THE PAST SPEAK, ONE DAY AT A TIME.

text:
The Green Corn Ceremony: the Southeastern New Year

When the first ears of corn ripened in mid or late summer, Muscogee (muss-KOH-gee), Cherokee (CHAIR-oh-kee), Seminole, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Yuchi, and related nations held a multi-day rite of purification and renewal. Outsiders called it the Busk, from a Muscogee word for “to fast” (poskita or puskita). It marked the start of the new year.
Among the Muscogee the basic community was the talwa (TAHL-wah), the town. Each talwa was a self-governing settlement with its own leadership, fields, and square ground. The mekko (MEK-ko), the town’s civil leader, and his council set the date for the ceremony. Larger or more important talwa often ran an eight-day form; smaller or daughter towns used a shorter four-day version. People from the talwa and its related settlements camped around the square.

The plaza was swept and sprinkled with white sand. Four open arbors faced the directions. Four logs were laid crosswise at the center and a new fire was kindled by friction. All old fires had been put out. Coals from the new fire later relit household hearths.

Men fasted. Women of the Turkey clan danced while a strong emetic was prepared. Men drank the black drink (yaupon holly tea, called the white drink by the people), which acted as a purgative. They rubbed ashes from the new fire on the chin, neck, and belly, then went to water. Women prepared the new corn. Men rubbed some of it on their faces and chests before anyone ate. Most wrongs short of murder were forgiven. A portion of the first crop was offered to the fire. Dances followed, including the turkey dance, ribbon dance, feather dance, and all-night stomp dances with call-and-response singing and women’s turtle-shell shakers. Many moved counterclockwise in sets of four.

Cherokee tradition links the gift of cultivated corn to Selu (SAY-loo), Corn Woman, and her husband Kanati (kah-NAH-tee), the Lucky Hunter. In the story, Selu produces corn from her body. When her sons misunderstand the power and kill her, she instructs them how to treat her body so that corn will grow where her blood falls, but only where people prepare the ground and tend the crop. The Green Corn rites recognize that gift and the labor required to keep it.

Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century observers documented versions of the ceremony while it was still held on ancestral grounds. Trader James Adair, naturalist William Bartram, Indian agent Benjamin Hawkins, and playwright John Howard Payne all left accounts. Payne’s 1835 description of the last Busk held by Creek towns in Alabama, just before removal, remains one of the most detailed. 

Anthropologists and ethnohistorians connect the practice to earlier Mississippian ceremonial life at square grounds and mound centers.

Similar first-fruits and new-year resets appear elsewhere. Chinese communities traditionally settle debts and clean houses before the lunar New Year. Hawaiian Makahiki was a multi-month harvest and peace period when warfare stopped and social accounts were closed. The Babylonian Akitu renewed cosmic order and the king’s mandate through purification, recitation of the creation epic, and a formal reset of authority. 

Parallel rites occur among some West African and Andean highland groups, where the new staple is not freely eaten until offerings and cleansing are complete. 

The Green Corn pattern is not unique in combining harvest gratitude, purification, and a limited amnesty, but it is distinctive in its tight link to corn, the square-ground setting, and its documented continuity through removal into the present.

After the removals of the 1830s the Muscogee and others reestablished ceremonial grounds in Indian Territory. Versions of the Green Corn Ceremony continue today at traditional grounds in Oklahoma and elsewhere. The core sequence of cleaning, forgiveness, new fire, and the first eating of the corn has remained stable even as some public details have been kept private.

Image: John White, A Festive Dance, 1585. Watercolor. British Museum. Shows a ceremonial dance circle with carved posts among coastal North Carolina peoples, long associated with harvest or Green Corn rites.

NFL 🏈 Houston Texans vs. Jacksonville Jaguars (October 18, 4:30 PM)

Current Polymarket valuation:

🐆 Jacksonville Jaguars - 58¢
🐂 Houston Texans - 43¢

The market views the Jaguars as roughly a 58% favorite. Betting lines also list Jacksonville as a slight favorite (around -3 points), suggesting the market expects a close game. However, the Texans offer interesting value at 43¢ not because they are the stronger team, but because the gap between the two sides is narrower than the market implies.

Jacksonville Jaguars strengths:

1. Strong team form - The Jaguars started the season confidently (4-1), displaying consistent play in key moments and solid efficiency metrics on both offense and defense, making them one of the most stable teams right now.
2. Trevor Lawrence is a key factor - He possesses a strong arm and good mobility, handles pressure well, and has experience in big games; in a high-scoring shootout scenario, his experience gives him an edge.
3. The Jaguars' defense is a major asset - They effectively pressure the quarterback, stop third-down conversions, and limit big passing plays factors that are particularly important against the Texans, who rely heavily on C.J. Stroud’s performance.
4. Home-field advantage + London - The Jaguars were already in London last week for their game against the Eagles, so their adjustment to the time zone and playing conditions may be smoother, giving them a slight advantage.

Jacksonville Jaguars weaknesses:

1. Jaguars' offense - Despite a strong start to the season, the team occasionally struggles with long scoreless streaks, a reliance on big plays, and errors in the red zone. 
2. Market assessment: Despite the Jaguars' strong start, the 58¢ rate on Polymarket implies a roughly 58% probability of victory, whereas the team's actual valuation likely falls in the 52–55% range, indicating a slight market overvaluation.

Houston Texans strengths:

1. C.J. Stroud: He is the Texans' biggest asset, he demonstrates precision as a quarterback with excellent ability to read defenses, rarely commits major errors, and has looked stronger this season than the team's overall record suggests.
2. Texans' offensive potential: The team boasts a potent arsenal of weapons, including Nico Collins who wins contested catches and poses a threat in the red zone and speedy receivers like Tank Dell, given enough time for Stroud, the offense is capable of putting up big numbers.

text:
Tyrant Tina's post treats “one-third of Oregonians (and half the kids) on the Oregon Health Plan” as a triumph of her protection rather than the clearest possible evidence that the state’s economy and policy choices have made private life unaffordable for a huge share of residents.

That’s the actual question: why is a third of the state dependent on a means-tested government program in the first place? Celebrating the size of the Medicaid rolls while accusing an opponent of “defunding” them for voting against HB 2010 (a 2025 extension of assessments/taxes on health-plan premiums, hospitals, and managed care organizations to fund OHP and related programs) is pure campaign spin. The bill passed; it was requested by Tyrant Tina; some Republicans supported it; Drazan and others opposed the tax mechanism and process. Voting against one more layer of provider taxes that get passed through to premiums and costs is not the same as voting to yank coverage from kids. Framing it that way is the usual “oppose my tax = want people to die” routine.

Oregon’s OHP enrollment sits in the 1.3–1.46 million range on a population of roughly 4.3 million about 30–34%, the “one in three” figure Kotek uses. That is high relative to many states and reflects deliberate policy choices: early and aggressive ACA expansion to 138% of the federal poverty level, further widening via the OHP Bridge program (up to 200% FPL), Healthier Oregon expansions covering illegal aliens, pandemic-era continuous eligibility that delayed redeterminations, and a relatively generous benefit package that draws federal matching dollars (often well above the base 50%). Enrollment more than doubled over the past decade or so while population growth was far slower. Human-services spending grew faster than education, and the program is richer than what many other blue states offer.

Meanwhile, the private market looks exactly like what you’d expect when government expands the free/near-free option and layers on regulations, mandates, and taxes. Marketplace bronze plans for a 40-year-old run hundreds of dollars a month at full price; silver benchmarks are higher; average net premiums after assistance jumped sharply once enhanced federal credits expired (from $272 to $426 monthly in the recent report); individual and small-group rates have seen repeated high-single-digit to double-digit hikes; carriers have exited. Housing costs, overall cost of living, and the long Democratic policy mix (high minimum wages, land-use rules, taxes, and the Measure 110 experiment’s aftermath) make it harder for middle- and working-class households to clear the income thresholds without falling back on the state plan. Half the kids on it is not a success story of “access” it’s intergenerational dependence created by the same dynamics.

The real affordability problem is that private coverage and employment-based insurance have been made expensive or unattractive for a large share of the population while the political response is to enlarge the government plan and then demand more taxes and federal match to sustain it. Opposing the next tax extension doesn’t “defund health care”; it questions whether endlessly expanding the dependency pool, rather than lowering the cost of living and the price of private coverage, is the path to people managing their own lives. Kotek’s post skips that entirely.

For fiscal responsibility and sanity VOTE @ChristineDrazan for governor in November
